items.comment: Grotius, DGP II.15.16 holds that the sovereign is bound in no way by a treaty a public person made without his order, so the Roman people owed the Samnites neither indemnity nor restoration of the position before the Caudine accord. Vattel accepts the Caudine conclusion but requires a sovereign who refuses ratification to restore whatever the other party handed over under the accord, since keeping it would be holding another's property without title. He requires prompt disavowal, and holds that equity obliges the state to ratify or to make a new fair treaty when the enemy acted generously, and forbids refusing an equitable and honourable treaty only to save the price of deliverance. He limits to things actually received the argument from the advantage gained, which Barbeyrac's note reports from Thomasius.
items.passage: le souverain de ce général doit sans doute restituer ce qu'il a reçu, s'il ne veut pas ratifier l'accord
items.sourcePassage: le Souverain n'est lié en aucune maniére par des Traitez ainsi conclus sans son ordre

items.question: Are the sovereign's and the state's debts binding on the nation, and within what limits?
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 479 holds that debts the ruler contracts with private persons for the cause of the republic bind successors and people, with the agreed interest. Vattel accepts the rule but limits it. Ruinous debts contracted without necessity do not bind the nation, and a sovereign without the power to tax has no power to create national debts.
items.passage: le conducteur, le souverain à qui elle n'a point confié le droit de lui imposer des taxes, des contributions, de faire, en un mot, de son autorité des levées de deniers, n'a point non plus le droit de l'obliger par ses emprunts, de créer des dettes à l'état
items.sourcePassage: si Rector civitatis aes alienum, a privatis Reip. causa suscipit, successores quoque et populus ad id luendum et usuras, utpote in se non illicitas (§. 1406. part. 4. Jur. nat.), conventas solvendum tenentur

items.locus: Droit de la guerre et de la paix, Liv. II ch. XIV § 13
items.question: Can the state or the successor revoke a sovereign's donations and privileges (as against his debts)?
items.comment: Grotius, DGP II.14.13 holds that favours a king grants from his own property have the force of a perfect donation and can be revoked only as punishment of a subject or for public utility, with compensation where possible, while mere dispensations from a law remain revocable. Vattel treats the sovereign's donations as gifts of state property, made without power when made without public cause, so that the successor or the state may always revoke them without compensation, and he classes gratuitous privileges with such donations. He reserves protection against revocation, save for abuse or the safety of the state and then with compensation, to immunities granted for cause, which he assimilates to onerous contracts.
items.passage: Le successeur ou l'état peut toujours révoquer une pareille donation
items.sourcePassage: Ces sortes de concessions ne peuvent (b) point être révoquées, à moins que ce ne soit, lors qu'il s'agit de Sujets, en forme de punition, ou pour l'utilité publique

items.question: What are pledges, engagements, hypothecs and antichresis between nations?
items.comment: Wolff, Institutiones § 1150 holds that when a whole province or part of the territory is handed over as security, an antichretic pact is joined to the pledge. Vattel treats the delivery of a town or province as an engagement and calls the pact antichresis only when the revenues are ceded in place of the interest. For Vattel the right to the revenues requires a separate cession and does not follow from the delivery itself.
items.passage: et si on lui en cede les revenus, en équivalant de l'intérêt de la dette, c'est le pacte qu'on appelle d'antichrese.
items.sourcePassage: Enimvero si integra provincia, aut certa territorii pars in securitatem crediti, vel quacunque de causa debiti traditur; pactum antichresticum ad oppignorationem accedit.

items.question: What are pledges, engagements, hypothecs and antichresis between nations?
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 485 holds that a province or part of the territory handed over as security carries an antichretic pact by that fact, since the only purpose of delivery beyond a hypothec and a garrison is to draw the revenues in lieu of interest. Vattel holds that the creditor who receives the place holds it by title of engagement, and that antichresis exists only if the revenues are ceded to him as the equivalent of interest. Wolff infers the cession of revenues from the delivery. Vattel requires it to be agreed.
items.passage: et si on lui en cede les revenus, en équivalant de l'intérêt de la dette, c'est le pacte qu'on appelle d'antichrese.
items.sourcePassage: Si integra provincia, aut certa territorii pars in securitatem pecuniae creditae, vel alia quacunque de causa debitae traditur; pactum antichresticum ad oppignorationem accedit.

items.question: What is pledged in a hostage, and what may be done to him if the giver defaults?
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 532 holds that if the giver defaults the hostage either becomes a slave or is held as a captive, but may not be killed. Vattel holds that only the liberty of hostages is pledged and that on default they may be kept in captivity. Vattel drops reduction to slavery and gives captivity as the only consequence.
items.passage: La liberté seule des otages est engagée ; et si celui qui les a donnés manque à sa parole , on peut les retenir en captivité.
items.sourcePassage: obses vel fit servus, vel tanquam captivus retinetur, interfici autem nequit.

items.locus: Droit de la guerre et de la paix, Liv. III ch. XX § 55
items.question: May hostages be retained for another claim once the promise they secured is fulfilled?
items.comment: Grotius, DGP III.20.55 holds that hostages given for one cause cannot be kept as hostages for another, but that if the giver has broken faith in another matter or incurred another debt they may be held under the rule of the law of nations that permits seizing subjects for their sovereign's act, unless an express clause provides for their return. Vattel denies any retention for another cause and names Grotius and Wolff as the authors he rejects. He grants the right to seize subjects but holds that the hostage is in the holder's power only by the faith of the treaty, which permits no use beyond the one agreed.
items.passage: Il n'est donc point permis de les retenir pour un autre sujet.
items.sourcePassage: les Otages donnez peuvent alors être retenus, non comme Otages, mais en conséquence de cette régle du Droit des Gens

items.question: May a hostage be retained for his own acts or debts incurred while a hostage?
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 505 holds that a hostage may be retained as a debtor until the costs of his maintenance are repaid and the debts he contracted are paid. Vattel holds that a hostage may be retained for his own acts, including offences committed against the nation that keeps him, as well as for debts contracted in the country. Vattel extends the ground of retention from contractual debt to delict.
items.passage: Mais on peut retenir un otage pour ses propres faits , pour des attentats commis, ou pour des dettes contractées dans le pays, pendant qu'il est en otage.
items.sourcePassage: quamdiu impensae in alimenta factae non fuerint restitutae, nec debita, quae obses contraxit, soluta, obses retineri potest ut debitor.

items.locus: Droit de la guerre et de la paix, Liv. III ch. XX § 54
items.question: May a hostage escape from the party holding him?
items.comment: Grotius, DGP III.20.54 holds that a hostage who has not given his word may escape without wrong, since the state that gives him only hands him over to be guarded as the enemy sees fit, though the state may not receive and keep him. Vattel holds that the hostage must stay faithfully with the holder and not try to escape, because the intention presumed in his sovereign is that he be kept until the promise is fully performed. Both require the state to return a fugitive hostage. Vattel follows Barbeyrac's note, which sides with Buddeus and Battier against Grotius.
items.passage: L'otage , de son côté , répondant à l'intention qui est à présumer dans son souverain, doit demeurer fidélement chez celui à qui il est remis , sans chercher à s'évader.
items.sourcePassage: Autrement il semble que l'intention de l'Etat, en donnant quelcun pour otage, ne soit pas (1) de lui imposer l'obligation de ne pas s'enfuïr, mais seulement de le remettre entre les mains de l'Ennemi, avec pouvoir de le garder comme il l'entendra.

items.locus: Droit de la guerre et de la paix, Liv. III ch. XX § 56
items.question: What happens to the obligation of a hostage and his substitute when one of them dies?
items.comment: Grotius, DGP III.20.56 holds that a person given as hostage to redeem a prisoner or another hostage is freed as soon as that other dies, because the right of the pledge ends with the death of the person pledged, and he approves Demetrius's claim to release after the death of Antiochus, for whom he had been given in exchange. Vattel frees the substitute on the hostage's natural death only where he took the hostage's place for a time. Where the hostage was exchanged for another, Vattel holds the first wholly free and the replacement alone bound, so the distinction between temporary substitution and exchange withdraws Grotius's release in the case of exchange.
items.passage: Ce seroit tout le contraire , si l'otage avoit été échangé pour un autre : le premier seroit absolument libre de tout engagement , & celui qui l'auroit remplacé, seroit seul lié.
items.sourcePassage: il est quitte de son obligation, du moment que cet autre vient à mourir.

items.question: What happens to a hostage who succeeds to the crown
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 519 holds that a hostage who succeeds to the giver's throne is freed once another suitable person is put in his place, since the receiver never acquired a right to hold the king. Vattel holds the same release on substitution of an equivalent security, but only where the giving state has kept the treaty. If that state has broken its word, Vattel allows the receiver to take advantage of the succession and keep the more valuable hostage.
items.passage: En cas que cet état eut manqué à sa parole , on profiteroit avec raison d'un événement qui lui rendroit l'otage beaucoup plus précieux , et sa délivrance plus nécessaire.
items.sourcePassage: alio idoneo in locum sui substituto ipse liberatur.

items.question: What is the fate of the hostage when the giver breaks faith
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 532 holds that when the giver breaks faith the hostage either becomes a slave or is held as a captive. Vattel holds that the hostage becomes a prisoner who may be kept in perpetual captivity, and adds that, being released from all obligation to the sovereign who abandoned him, he may give himself as a subject to his keeper or be freed on agreed terms. Vattel omits slavery and dissolves the hostage's bond to his own sovereign.
items.passage: Et comme l'otage n'est plus tenu à rien envers le souverain, qui l'a abandonné par une perfidie , s'il veut se donner à celui qui est devenu le maître de sa destinée , celui - ci pourra acquérir un sujet utile , au lieu d'un prisonnier misérable , objet importun de sa commisération.
items.sourcePassage: obses vel fit servus, vel tanquam captivus retinetur, interfici autem nequit.

items.locus: Droit de la guerre et de la paix, Liv. II ch. XVI § 10
items.question: What the distinction between favourable and odious matters is, and how it guides extension or restriction of indeterminate terms
items.comment: Grotius, DGP II.16.10 defines favourable matters by their content, as those that involve equality or tend to common utility, and odious matters as those burdensome to one party, penal, annulling an act or altering what was settled. Vattel defends the distinction against Barbeyrac, who rejected it, but defines it by its interpretive effect: favourable matters are those where equity is better kept by extending the terms, odious those where restriction serves equity better. He confines the distinction to cases where the precise intention cannot be fixed by the other rules of interpretation.
items.passage: Les choses odieuses , au contraire , sont celles dont la restriction tend plus sûrement à l'équité , que leur extension.
items.sourcePassage: Les Favorables sont celles qui renferment de l'égalité, ou celles qui tendent à (2) l'Utilité commune

items.locus: Droit de la guerre et de la paix, Liv. II ch. XVI § 10
items.question: How things partly favorable and partly odious are to be classed (which side prevails)
items.comment: Grotius, DGP II.16.10, holds that a thing partly favourable and partly odious counts as one or the other according to the size of the good and of the change, and that other things being equal the favourable side prevails. Vattel counts a mixed thing as favourable only when its good far exceeds its odious side, and ranks it among odious things when the two balance. The point of difference is the rule for the even case, which Vattel reverses on the ground that in doubt one must take the course least likely to injure equity.
items.passage: Mais à moins de cette disproportion , & toutes choses d'ailleurs égales , la faveur est pour le parti qui n'offre rien d'odieux
items.sourcePassage: le reste d'ailleurs égal, le Favorable l'emporte.

items.question: Examples: whether 'allies' in a treaty includes future allies; the liberty promised to Carthage
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 670 holds that allies named in a treaty are only those allied at the time, not future allies, unless the treaty says so expressly, because interpretation follows what the parties probably had in mind. Vattel holds that a clause binding each party not to harm the other's allies is favourable and must be extended to all present and future allies. Vattel decides the scope of the word by the favourable or odious character of the clause, not by the parties' probable thought at the time of contracting.
items.passage: et sur ce pied-là , il est si favorable à tous égards , si conforme à l'humanité et aux sentimens qui doivent unir deux alliés qu'on doit sans difficulté l'étendre à tous les alliés présens et à venir.
items.sourcePassage: socii tantum intelliguntur, qui nunc sunt, non vero futuri, nisi expresse dicatur, et qui nunc sunt, et qui futuri sunt.

items.locus: Droit de la guerre et de la paix, Liv. II ch. XVI § 13
items.question: Whether "allies" in a treaty clause (Rome-Carthage) covers future allies, and whether such a clause is odious
items.comment: Grotius, DGP II.16.13, holds that the Roman-Carthaginian clause protecting each party's allies cannot extend to allies made after the treaty, because the extension would concern the rupture of an alliance, an odious matter, and would restrict the natural liberty to make war. Vattel treats the clause as favourable and extends it to all allies present and future. He denies that it is odious on either of Grotius's grounds, since it leaves intact the right to make war on an ally who gives just cause. Vattel follows Barbeyrac's note, which extends the clause to future allies.
items.passage: il est si favorable à tous égards , si conforme à l'humanité & aux sentimens qui doivent unir deux alliés qu'on doit sans difficulté l'étendre à tous les alliés présens & à venir
items.sourcePassage: on ne pouvoit pas expliquer le terme d'Alliez contenu dans le Traité d'une maniére qui s'étendît à ceux qui ne l'étoient pas encore alors

items.locus: Droit de la guerre et de la paix, Liv. II ch. XVI § 29
items.question: When two duties are in concurrence, does the one of higher honesty and utility prevail?
items.comment: Grotius, DGP II.16.29, gives preference among conflicting provisions to the one founded on reasons of greater honesty or utility. Vattel keeps the rule for duties in competition but confines it to duties equally within our power and choice. In his view an earlier engagement removes the competition, so the older ally's claim to aid prevails over the more praiseworthy defence of another nation unless a new ally faces certain ruin.
items.passage: Mais elle regarde les devoirs qui sont également en notre puissance , & pour ainsi dire , à notre choix
items.sourcePassage: Il faut donner la préférence à ce qui est fondé (8) sur des raisons ou des vuës, qui renferment un plus grand degré d'Honnêteté, ou d'Utilité.

items.question: Rule 9: whether a sworn treaty prevails over an unsworn one in a collision
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 427 holds that an oath induces no obligation beyond the one arising from the treaty, so swearing gives a treaty no right of precedence. Vattel holds that the oath adds new force to the obligation, so that a sworn treaty prevails over an unsworn one when other things are equal. Both keep the priority of the earlier ally, but Vattel makes the oath a ground of preference that Wolff denies.
items.passage: parce que le serment ajoute une nouvelle force à l'obligation
items.sourcePassage: Juramentum enim non aliam inducit obligationem, quam quae ex foedere oritur

items.locus: Droit de la guerre et de la paix, Liv. II ch. XVI § 29
items.question: Does a treaty confirmed by oath prevail over an unsworn treaty in conflict?
items.comment: Grotius, DGP II.16.29, holds that a sworn convention prevails over an unsworn one in conflict, because of the religious act that accompanies it. Vattel lets the sworn treaty prevail only other things being equal, on the ground that the oath adds force to the obligation. He adds that the oath does not change the nature of treaties and so cannot give a new ally precedence over an older ally whose treaty is unsworn.
items.passage: Mais comme il ne change rien à la nature des traités ; ( §§. 225. & suiv. ) il ne peut , par exemple , donner l'avantage à un nouvel allié sur un allié plus ancien , dont le traité ne sera pas juré.
items.sourcePassage: si en certaines circonstances il y a du conflict entre une Convention faite avec serment, & une autre sans serment ; la prémiére (10) doit l'emporter, à cause de l'acte religieux (11) qui l'accompagne.

items.question: How freely a nation or its ruler may waive rights and grievances
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 568 holds that every nation may waive its grievances and dispose of its right as it sees fit or as prudence advises. Vattel holds that the sovereign is only the administrator of the nation's rights and may dispose of them only as the nation would presumably do. Vattel adds a limit on the ruler's discretion that Wolff's rule for the nation does not contain.
items.passage: Les droits de la nation sont des biens dont le souverain n'est que l'administrateur ; il ne doit en disposer que comme il a lieu de présumer que la nation en disposeroit elle - même.
items.sourcePassage: Unamquamque Gentem de jure suo disponere posse, prouti sibi visum fuerit, vel prudentia suadet

items.question: Whether and when parties are bound by an arbitral award
items.comment: Wolff, Institutiones § 770 holds that the parties to a compromise are bound to acquiesce in the arbiter's award. Vattel holds that a manifestly unjust award, or one exceeding the matter submitted, does not bind the parties. The exception for manifest injustice and excess of mandate is absent from Wolff's rule.
items.passage: si par une sentence manifestement injuste et contraire à la raison, les arbitres s'étoient eux-mêmes dépouillés de leur qualité, leur jugement ne mériteroit aucune attention
items.sourcePassage: Partes igitur litigantes in laudo acquiescere tenentur

items.question: May a nation take arms without first trying conciliation
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 574 holds that under the voluntary law of nations arms may be taken without first trying conference or compromise, and that each nation's own judgment on the matter must stand. Vattel admits the same permission but requires the sovereign to be able to justify before the world that the offers of peace are a ruse. He denies that a nation's mere suspicions suffice, where Wolff leaves the judgment to each nation.
items.passage: Prétendre s'autoriser de ses seuls soupçons, c'est ébranler tous les fondemens de la sûreté des nations.
items.sourcePassage: standum sit uniuscujusque de istis judicio

items.locus: Droit de la guerre et de la paix, Liv. II ch. XXIII § 11
items.question: May one take arms to obtain a thing to which one has only a doubtful right, against a possessor?
items.comment: Grotius, DGP II.23.11, holds that a claimant without titles sufficient to convict the possessor of unjust possession cannot lawfully make war on him, and that both parties must seek accommodation, the claimant more than the possessor. Vattel equally forbids taking arms to gain possession on a doubtful right. He permits arms to compel the possessor to discuss the claim, accept a reasonable means of decision or settle on equitable terms. The point of difference is this permission, which makes war lawful against a possessor who refuses such means, a case Grotius's section does not admit.
items.passage: On peut seulement obliger le possesseur même, s'il le faut, par les armes, à discuter la question, à accepter quelque moyen raisonnable de décision, ou d'accommodement ; ou enfin à transiger sur un pied équitable.
items.sourcePassage: si l'on n'a pas en main des titres suffisans pour convaincre le Possesseur de l'injustice de sa possession, on ne peut pas légitimement lui déclarer la Guerre pour ce sujet

items.question: Which goods may be seized in reprisals
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 495 holds that the goods of citizens are naturally bound for the debts of their nation, without exception. Vattel draws the same rule for reprisals but exempts a deposit entrusted to the public faith, such as foreign money placed in the public funds.
items.passage: pourvû que ce ne soit pas un dépôt confié à la foi publique
items.sourcePassage: Bona civium seu subditorum obligata sunt naturaliter pro debitis civitatis, seu Gentis.

items.question: Who indemnifies the subject whose goods are taken in reprisals
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 598 holds that those who gave cause to reprisals must indemnify the fellow citizens who suffer by them, since within the state one citizen's act cannot be imputed to another. Vattel holds that the sovereign must indemnify the subject on whom reprisals fall, because the loss is a debt of the state of which each citizen bears only his share. The two assign the duty of compensation to different parties on different grounds.
items.passage: c'est alors au souverain à dédommager celui de ses sujets sur qui sont tombées les représailles ; c'est une dette de l'état ou de la nation, dont chaque citoyen ne doit supporter que sa quote-part.
items.sourcePassage: Qui causam dederunt repressaliis, damna iis resarcire debent, quibus eam ob causam aliquid decedit.

items.locus: Droit de la guerre et de la paix, Liv. III ch. II § 7
items.question: Who may order and carry out reprisals (the sovereign only, or private persons)?
items.comment: Grotius, DGP III.2.7, holds that the law of nations permits any person to take reprisals, and that only the civil laws of some countries require leave from the sovereign or the ordinary judges. Vattel holds that only sovereigns may exercise and order reprisals, because the goods of private persons count as the nation's only between state and state and because reprisals border on open war. The point of difference is the source of the requirement of the sovereign's leave, which Grotius places in civil law and Vattel in the law of nations. Vattel's second ground follows Barbeyrac's note, which requires the sovereign's permission because reprisals are a step toward war.
items.passage: Il n'appartient donc qu'aux souverains d'exercer & d'ordonner les représailles
items.sourcePassage: Le Droit des Gens permet à chacun (2) d'user du droit de Représailles

items.question: What counts as a refusal of justice justifying reprisals
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 587 holds that the civil-law presumption of a confirmed sentence's justice does not hold between nations, so that a foreign sentence is not taken as just whether well or badly given. Vattel holds that the law of nations requires reciprocal regard for foreign jurisdiction for the same reason as the civil-law presumption, and obliges subjects to submit to foreign sentences in all doubtful cases. Both treat a manifestly unjust sentence as a denial of justice, but Vattel extends to nations the presumption that Wolff rejects.
items.passage: Le droit des gens prescrit aux nations ces égards réciproques pour la jurisdiction de chacune, par la même raison que la loi civile ordonne dans l'état, de tenir pour juste toute sentence définitive renduedans les formes.
items.sourcePassage: inter Gentes sententia judicis seu bene, seu male prolata pro vera et justa non habetur, etiamsi a superiore fuerit confirmata.

items.locus: Droit de la guerre et de la paix, Liv. III ch. II § 6
items.question: May force, even to the point of killing, be used against those who resist just reprisals?
items.comment: Grotius, DGP III.2.6, allows the killing of those who resist reprisals only by accident and holds that charity requires abandoning the claim when one foresees having to kill. Vattel holds that a sovereign may repel resisters even at the cost of their lives, and names Grotius in rejecting his rule. He confines Grotius's counsel to private persons in matters of small importance and makes the true good of the state the rule between sovereigns. Vattel takes the side of Barbeyrac's note, which rejects Grotius's rule as making reprisals useless against resolute resisters.
items.passage: Il est donc permis de repousser ceux qui entreprennent de s'opposer à de justes représailles, & s'il faut pour cela aller jusqu'à leur ôter la vie, on ne peut accuser de ce malheur que leur résistance injuste & inconsidérée.
items.sourcePassage: quand on prévoit que l'on sera réduit à en venir là, la Charité veut qu'on néglige (2) plûtôt la poursuite de son droit

items.question: Must reprisals be preferred to war, and when is war rather than reprisal required?
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 606 holds that war may not be declared while reprisals can repair the injury or obtain satisfaction, and that war becomes just when reprisals cannot. Vattel keeps the preference for reprisals but holds that in a dispute over a contested right, as opposed to a wrong received, reprisals are condemnable and a declaration of war must follow. Wolff draws no such distinction between kinds of dispute.
items.passage: Lorsqu'il s'agit dans le différend, non d'une voie de fait, d'un tort reçu, mais d'un droit contesté ; après que l'on a inutilement tenté les voies de conciliation, ou les moyens pacifiques d'obtenir justice, c'est la déclaration de guerre qui doit suivre, et non de prétendues représailles
items.sourcePassage: quamdiu autem per illas injuria reparari, aut ob irreparabilem satisfactio obtineri potest, bellum parti adversae indicere naturaliter non licet

items.question: Is every citizen obliged to bear arms for the state?
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 749 holds that all subjects able to serve are bound to military service only in a case of extreme necessity, and that outside that case those useful to the state in other callings are not bound and are not to be conscripted. Vattel holds that every citizen able to bear arms must take them at the first command of the holder of the war power. Vattel makes the obligation itself unconditional and leaves the sparing of useful citizens to the prudence of government (III.10), where Wolff limits the obligation itself.
items.passage: Quiconque est en état de porter les armes , doit les prendre , au premier commandement de celui qui a le pouvoir de faire la guerre.
items.sourcePassage: ita nec omnes promiscue ad operas militares praestandas obligantur, nisi extrema adfuerit necessitas

items.question: Whom may the sovereign enrol, and by what means?
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 749 holds that outside extreme necessity those able to render other useful services and to contribute to war costs are not to be conscripted, and that a levy contrary to this is an abuse of the right of conscription. Vattel holds that the sovereign may enrol whomever he pleases in time of need, and only advises him to choose fit men and, where possible, volunteers. Wolff's restriction is a limit of right, Vattel's preference for volunteers is a counsel of propriety.
items.passage: Puisque tout citoyen ou sujet est obligé de servir l'état , le souverain est en droit d'enrôler qui il lui plaît , dans le besoin.
items.sourcePassage: extra hunc casum milites conscribendi non sunt, qui alias Reip. utiles ac necessarias operas praestare et ad sumtus bellicos contribuere possunt

items.question: Who is exempt from bearing arms (women, clergy, magistrates)?
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 752 holds that nature does not bar women from military service, since experience shows they are not unfit for it by reason of sex. Vattel exempts women as a class, on the ground that rules must follow what is ordinary, that women are needed for other tasks, and that mixing the sexes in armies is inconvenient. Both deny the clergy any natural exemption; they differ on women.
items.passage: Par cette raison , on exempte les vieillards , les enfanset les femmes.
items.sourcePassage: Foeminas a bellorum ministerio non arcet natura, quas propter sexum ad id non esse ineptas, experientia comprobat

items.question: Liability of a subordinate who falsely claims power
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 774 holds that a subordinate power which claims a greater right than it has is liable to the deceived party both for the damage and to punishment, and may also be punished by its sovereign. Vattel holds the subordinate liable only to repair the damage, and assigns punishment to its own sovereign as a duty of justice. The deceived party's own right to punish drops out.
items.passage: elle est naturellement tenue du dommage causé par sa fraude , et obligée à le réparer.
items.sourcePassage: tenetur ei, cum quo actum est, non modo de damno per demonstrata n. 1. verum etiam ad poenam.

items.locus: Droit de la guerre et de la paix, Liv. III ch. XXII § 4
items.question: What follows when a subordinate falsely claims a power he lacks and deceives the other party (even an enemy)?
items.comment: Grotius, DGP III.22.4 holds that a public minister who falsely claims greater powers must pay the value of what he promised and repair the damage, answering with his goods and failing them with servitude or prison, and may also be punished in person or goods according to the gravity of the fraud. Vattel holds the faithless officer bound to repair the damage caused by his fraud and lays the duty of punishing him and compelling reparation on his own sovereign, as a debt to justice and to that sovereign's glory. Vattel thus moves the punishment of the deceiving officer from the party he deceived to his own sovereign.
items.passage: Le souverain de cet officier de mauvaise foi , doit le punir & l'obliger à réparer sa faute , il le doit à la justice & à sa propre gloire.
items.sourcePassage: Pour l'autre, on est en droit de s'en prendre ou à sa personne, ou à ses biens, ou à l'un & l'autre tout ensemble, selon la grandeur du crime.

items.question: How can defence become just against an originally just offensive war?
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 629 holds without exception that defensive war against a just offensive war is unjust, and requires the wrongdoer to offer equitable terms before open combat. Vattel holds that once just satisfaction has been offered and refused, the attacker's hostilities become unjust and the defender's arms just. Vattel makes the refused offer a condition that converts the justice of the war, where Wolff states the offer only as a duty.
items.passage: l'on oppose désormais de justes armes à ses hostilités, devenues injustes, parce qu'elles n'ont plus de fondement
items.sourcePassage: injustum vero est defensivum si offensivum fuerit justum

items.question: When a war is nonetheless held legitimate on both sides (good faith, doubtful cause, invincible error)
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 634 holds that only one side's arms are just, that a party in good faith still does not act justly, and that in a doubtful cause the judgement on justice stays suspended even after victory. Vattel holds that in any doubtful cause the arms of both parties must pass as equally legitimate as to external effects until the cause is decided, on the ground of the equality and independence of nations. Vattel adds a rule of external legitimacy for both belligerents that Wolff's section does not admit.
items.passage: les armes des deux parties qui se font la guerre doivent passer également pour légitimes, au moins quant aux effets extérieurs, et jusqu'à ce que la cause soit décidée
items.sourcePassage: uterque bona quidem fide agit ; non tamen juste, cum juste agere nequeat nisi is, qui jure agit

items.locus: Droit de la guerre et de la paix, Liv. II ch. XXIII § 13
items.question: When must a war nevertheless be treated as legitimate on both sides (good faith, doubtful cause, external effects)?
items.comment: Grotius, DGP II.23.13 holds that a war cannot be just on both sides as to the action, that both parties may act without injustice through ignorance though in war some rashness or want of charity is hardly ever absent, and that wars are just on both sides only as to certain legal effects, which he refers to formal public wars. Vattel holds that in any doubtful cause the arms of both parties must pass as equally legitimate as to external effects until the cause is decided, because nations are equal and independent and cannot judge one another. Vattel grounds this bilateral legitimacy in the independence of nations and confines it to doubtful causes, where Grotius ties it to the forms of public war.
items.passage: Puis donc que les nations sont égales & indépendantes ( Liv. II. §. 36. & Prélim. §§. 18. 19. ) & ne peuvent s'ériger en juges les unes des autres, il s'ensuit que dans toute cause susceptible de doute, les armes des deux parties qui se font la guerre doivent passer également pour légitimes, au moins quant aux effets extérieurs, & jusqu'à ce que la cause soit décidée.
items.sourcePassage: Enfin, si l'on entend le mot de Juste par rapport à certains effets de droit, il est certain qu'en ce sens il y a des Guerres justes de part & d'autre; comme il paroîtra par ce que nous dirons ci-dessous des Guerres Publiques & dans les formes.

items.question: Whether and how appearances of danger from a rising neighbour give a right to use force preventively
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 650 grants the right to break a growing power by arms only when that nation openly plans to subjugate others and has already done an injury, however slight. Vattel sets aside the requirement of an injury received and allows a nation to demand securities, and to strike if they are refused, once a neighbour about to gain formidable power has given signs of injustice or ambition. The point of difference is the injury: Wolff makes an actual injury the condition, Vattel makes a reasonable presumption of ill will, weighed against the magnitude of the danger, sufficient.
items.passage: Dès qu'un état a donné des marques d'injustice, d'avidité, d'orgueil, d'ambition, d'un desir impérieux de faire la loi, c'est un voisin suspect, dont on doit se garder : on peut le prendre au moment où il est sur le point de recevoir un accroissement formidable de puissance, lui demander des sûretés, et s'il hésite à les donner, prévenir ses desseins par la force des armes
items.sourcePassage: si qua Gens consilia manifesta agitet de aliis Gentibus sibi subjiciendis, levissima injuria jus dat vi armata potentiam crescentem labefactandi

items.locus: Droit de la guerre et de la paix, Liv. III ch. III § 6
items.question: Is a declaration of war necessary before taking up arms, and on what ground?
items.comment: Grotius, DGP III.3.6 holds that natural law requires no declaration of war when one defends oneself, punishes the offender himself or merely retakes one's own, and that a prior summons in such cases is fine and praiseworthy but not owed. Vattel holds that after satisfaction has been refused a nation owes it to humanity and to the blood and repose of its subjects to declare to the unjust nation that it is about to use open force. Vattel turns Grotius's counsel into a duty of natural law, following Barbeyrac's note against Grotius that such a summons is obligatory whenever it can be made without prejudice.
items.passage: nous devons encore ce ménagement à l'humanité , & sur-tout au sang & au repos des sujets , de déclarer à cette nation injuste , ou à son conducteur , que nous allons enfin recourir au dernier remede & employer la force ouverte
items.sourcePassage: Selon le Droit Naturel, lors qu'il s'agit seulement de se défendre, ou de punir celui-là même qui s'est rendu coupable; il ne faut point de Déclaration de Guerre.

items.question: Does the right to make war lapse when equitable terms are offered
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 711 holds that when equitable terms of peace are offered to the party declaring war, they must be accepted and war abstained from. Vattel holds the same but requires that the offers be accompanied by security, since one need not be put off by empty proposals. He adds that a sovereign's word is sufficient security unless he is known to be perfidious.
items.passage: Bien entendu que les offres doivent être accompagnées de sûreté ; car on n'est point obligé de se laisser amuser par de vaines propositions.
items.sourcePassage: Quodsi ergo aequae conditiones offerantur bellum denuncianti ; cessat belli gerendi ratio, consequenter eaedem acceptandae et a bello abstinendum.

items.question: May the declaration be omitted in an offensive war when the enemy admits no envoy?
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 714 allows the declaration of an offensive war to be omitted only when the enemy admits no envoys, no letter can be sent and no third party can carry the declaration, the impossibility being the enemy's fault. Vattel holds that refusal to admit a minister or herald suffices, and that the declaration is then made by publication in one's own states or on the frontier. Vattel also excuses sending a herald where the enemy's treatment of envoys makes it dangerous.
items.passage: on peut , quelle que soit d'ailleurs la coutume , se contenter de la publier dans ses propres états , ou sur la frontiere
items.sourcePassage: Si is, cui bellum denunciandum, nec legatos admittit nec adsit occasio mittendi epistolam, nec denunciatio per tertium fieri possit; denunciatio belli offensivi omittenda.

items.question: What must the inhabitants do when a foreign army enters before war is declared?
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 718 holds that inhabitants must not resist an army that enters to declare war and announces peaceful intent, because its entry is lawful and resistance injures it. Vattel holds the same but adds that such an army may be refused entry into fortified places and cannot demand it. He grounds the inhabitants' restraint in their lack of the sovereign's order and lets them occupy advantageous posts and defend them if attacked.
items.passage: Bien entendu qu'on ne lui permettra point l'entrée dans les places fortes , et qu'il ne peut la demander.
items.sourcePassage: isto casu et incolae vi se eidem opponere non debent, qui vero hoc facere audeat, in eos licita animadversio.

items.locus: Droit de la guerre et de la paix, Liv. I ch. III § 4
items.question: What makes a war legitimate and in due form (sovereign authority plus formalities)?
items.comment: Grotius, DGP I.3.4 holds that a solemn war requires sovereign authority on each side and certain formalities, and that the two conditions are equally necessary. Vattel adopts the two conditions but exempts defensive war from the declaration and, in pressing occasions, from an express order of the sovereign. Grotius classes a war begun by a magistrate under pressing danger as public but not solemn, and in DGP III.3.12 he denies that defensive war can dispense with a declaration.
items.passage: car la guerre défensive n'a pas besoin d'une déclaration (§. 57.), ni même, dans les occasions pressantes, d'un ordre exprès du souverain
items.sourcePassage: Ces conditions sont également nécessaires, en sorte que, l'une manquant, l'autre demeure inutile.

items.question: Why legitimate war differs from brigandage (grounds of the distinction)
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 778 holds that whoever wages an unjust war is a robber, invader and brigand, since all force in an unjust war is without right. Vattel reserves the name of brigandage for war undertaken without any right and without even an apparent cause. A war declared in form over a dispute has, by the voluntary law of nations, the same effects on both sides whatever the justice of the cause.
items.passage: Entreprise sans aucun droit , sans sujet même apparent , elle ne peut produire aucun effet légitime , ni donner aucun droit à celui qui en est l'auteur.
items.sourcePassage: Qui bellum injustum gerit praedo, invasor ac latro est.

items.question: Status of immovables held by foreigners in enemy country, and enemy subjects' immovables at home
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 842 holds that immovables held in enemy territory by any foreigner, neutral or not, are hostile things, because the land is subject to the territorial jurisdiction. Vattel accepts the rule on the same ground but adds that modern usage grants safeguards to houses and lands held by foreigners in enemy country. The added usage removes most of the practical effect of the classification.
items.passage: on donne des sauve - gardes aux maisons, aux terres que des étrangers possedent en pays ennemi
items.sourcePassage: Immo in genere bona immobilia in territorio hostili possessa a peregrino res hostiles sunt.

items.question: Are debts owed to the enemy by third parties enemy property that may be seized or confiscated?
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 729 holds without qualification that whatever is owed to my enemy, even by a non-enemy debtor, counts among hostile things. Vattel accepts this in principle but exempts rights granted by a third party in which that party has an interest, such as rights of commerce. He also holds that general European usage now bars confiscating debts owed to the enemy, and that breaching this usage violates public faith.
items.passage: Et dès que cet usage est généralement reçu, celui qui y donneroit atteinte blesseroit la foi publique ; car les étrangers n'ont confié à ses sujets, que dans la ferme persuasion que l'usage général seroit observé.
items.sourcePassage: ea, quae debentur hosti meo, etiamsi debitor hostis non sit, in numero rerum hostilium sunt

items.locus: Droit de la guerre et de la paix, Liv. III ch. VIII § 4
items.question: Do incorporeal things (debts and rights owed by third parties to the enemy) count as enemy property open to war rights?
items.comment: Grotius, DGP III.8.4 holds that the incorporeal rights, names and actions of a conquered state pass to the victor as far as he chooses to appropriate them, since the master of a person is master of all his rights. Vattel counts the enemy's rights, names and actions among his goods but excepts rights granted by a third party who has an interest in who holds them, such as rights of commerce. Grotius states no such exception.
items.passage: ex-cepté cependant ces especes de droits qu'un tiers a concédés & qui l'intéressent, ensorte qu'il ne lui est pas indifférent par qui ils soient possédés
items.sourcePassage: Car quiconque est maître d'une personne, est maître aussi & des choses, & de tous les droits qui lui appartenoient.

items.question: Is there a tacit just-war clause in peacetime war alliances, and how far does it release the ally?
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 659 holds that every war alliance made in peacetime carries the tacit clause "if the war is just". Vattel accepts the clause but confines it to an evidently unjust war and requires the bound ally to presume his partner's cause just in doubtful cases. Wolff applies a manifest-injustice test only later, in Jus gentium § 662, and states no presumption in the ally's favour.
items.passage: La restriction tacite ne doit s'entendre que d'une guerre évidemment injuste ; autrement, on ne manqueroit jamais de prétexte pour éluder les traités.
items.sourcePassage: id quod omni factum intelligitur sub tacita hac clausula, si bellum fuerit justum

items.question: When does the casus foederis arise under a guarantee of possessions, and how is it determined?
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 662 holds that the casus foederis does not exist when the ally's arms are manifestly unjust, because of the tacit just-war clause. Vattel holds that under a guarantee of the ally's possessions the casus foederis arises on invasion, and that even against an attacker with a just cause the guarantor may refuse to let those possessions be taken while obliging the ally to give satisfaction. For guarantees the injustice of the ally's cause no longer cancels the obligation.
items.passage: Si quelqu'un les attaque pour une juste cause, il faut obliger l'allié à donner satisfaction, mais on est fondé à ne pas souffrir que ses possessions lui soient enlevées
items.sourcePassage: casus foederis non existit, si foederati manifesto injusta sunt arma

items.question: What is owed when allies of the same alliance fight each other, and what does 'allies reserved' cover?
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 669 holds that when members of the same alliance fight each other the treaty binds the third member to neither and gives neither any right. Vattel agrees that no aid is owed but holds that the alliance still obliges the third member to offer good offices for a reconciliation. Failing that, he leaves it free to aid the party in the right.
items.passage: L'alliance ne l'oblige donc à autre chose qu'à interposer ses bons offices, pour reconcilier ses alliés
items.sourcePassage: In praesenti nimirum casu neutri sociorum ex foedere obligaris, atque neutri ex eo jus quoddam quaesitum

items.question: Does assisting my enemy make one my enemy, and who counts as his associates?
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 730 holds that whoever associates with my enemy, by sending auxiliaries or subsidies or helping him in any way, is my enemy. Vattel cites this section and rejects the general rule as unsupported by principle and contrary to European usage. He holds that only those genuinely associated in the war count as enemies, so that supplying aid does not by itself make a state an enemy.
items.passage: Elle ne peut se soutenir par les principes, et l'usage de l'Europe s'y trouve heureusement contraire.
items.sourcePassage: Qui hosti meo se associat, veluti auxilia aut subsidia mittendo, aut quocunque modo eum in bello adjuvando; hostis meus est.

items.question: Are those who voluntarily aid my enemy without a treaty his associates (my enemies)?
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 730 holds that whoever aids my enemy in any way, by auxiliaries, subsidies or otherwise, is my enemy. Vattel holds that voluntary helpers are associates of the enemy, but that limited aid given by a nation which keeps friendly or neutral relations may be dissimulated, and that custom does not treat such aid, chiefly permission to levy volunteers, as an act of hostility. Vattel keeps the right intact and adds a customary practice of not exercising it against limited aid.
items.passage: Cette prudence, de ne pas rompre toujours ouvertement avec ceux qui assistent ainsi un ennemi, afin de ne les point obliger à se joindre à lui avec toutes leurs forces, ce ménagement, dis - je, a insensiblement introduit la coutume de ne pas regarder une pareille assistance, sur - tout quand elle ne consiste que dans la permission de lever des troupes volontaires, comme un acte d'hostilité.
items.sourcePassage: Qui hosti meo se associat, veluti auxilia aut subsidia mittendo, aut quocunque modo eum in bello adjuvando; hostis meus est.

items.question: Does a general defensive alliance made before the present war make the ally who aids my enemy an associate?
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 736 holds that an ally who sends any promised aid under a war alliance against all, concluded before the present war, becomes the enemy of his ally's adversary. Vattel holds that a general defensive alliance concluded before the war has this effect only if it promises assistance with all the allies' forces. Vattel makes the scale of the promised aid the condition of enemy status, which Wolff does not.
items.passage: L'alliance défensive, quoique générale et faite avant qu'il fût question de la guerre présente, produit encore le même effet, si elle porte une assistance de toutes les forces des alliés.
items.sourcePassage: Quodsi ergo vi foederis contra omnes jam ante initi, quam de bello praesente cogitaretur, auxilia, vel subsidia mittit, aut alio quocunque modo in bello adjuvet foederatum, hostis ejus existit, contra quem bellum geritur a foederato.

items.question: Does aid given under a prior defensive treaty not aimed at me make the helper nation my enemy and give just cause for war?
items.comment: Wolff, Institutiones § 1185 holds that whoever aids my enemy in any way, by auxiliaries or subsidies, is my enemy and his goods are hostile. Vattel holds that a nation furnishing determinate aid under an earlier defensive treaty not made against me pays a debt, does me no injury and gives me no just cause of war. For Vattel only the auxiliary troops it sends are my enemies, not the nation itself.
items.passage: les secours qu'ils fournissent à mon ennemi sont une dette qu'ils payent ; ils ne me font point injure en l'acquittant, et par conséquent ils ne me donnent aucun juste sujet de leur faire la guerre.
items.sourcePassage: Qui hosti meo se associat, veluti auxilia aut subsidia mittendo, aut eum quocunque modo in bello adjuvando , cum ad bellum ipsius concurrat , et ideo ejus particeps fiat ( §. 26. ) ; hostis meus est et res ejus hostiles sunt

items.question: Does aid given under a prior defensive treaty not aimed at me make the helper nation my enemy and give just cause for war?
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 733 holds that one may make war on whoever associates with my enemy, and that aid given to the party waging an unjust war is an injury that makes the helper equal to an aggressor. Vattel holds that treaty aid becomes an injury only where the ally's defensive war is manifestly unjust. In doubtful cases Vattel presumes in favour of the ally and treats both sides' arms as equally legitimate in external effects, so that the justice of the cause rarely decides.
items.passage: Un seul cas pourroit former ici une exception ; c'est celui d'une défensive manifestement injuste.
items.sourcePassage: sed qui quid facit in gratiam ejus, qui bellum injustum gerit, injuriam committit in eum, ex cujus parte bellum justum est

items.question: Must war be declared on the associates of the enemy?
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 734 holds that no denunciation is needed to make war on anyone who aids my enemy in any way, since such war counts as defensive. Vattel holds that no declaration is needed against true associates, but that nations aiding my enemy's defensive war without being his associates must first be asked for satisfaction and then declared against. The difference follows from Vattel's narrower class of associates.
items.passage: Je puis leur en demander raison, et si elles ne me satisfont pas, poursuivre mon droit et leur faire la guerre ; mais alors il faut la déclarer.
items.sourcePassage: Si bellum infertur ei, qui hosti meo se associat, veluti auxilia, aut subsidia mittendo, vel alio quocunque modo eum adjuvando: denunciatione opus non est.

items.locus: Droit de la guerre et de la paix, Liv. III ch. III § 10
items.question: Must war be declared on the associates of the enemy (and the Manlius-Galatians case)?
items.comment: Grotius, DGP III.3.10 holds that a war made after the main war on a people that aided the enemy requires a fresh declaration, and judges Manlius's war on the Galatians not lawful under the law of nations for want of one. Vattel holds that the Galatians had declared themselves enemies of Rome by supplying troops for an offensive war, and that Manlius waged the expedition as a continuation of the war with Antiochus, whose treaty was not yet consummated and did not cover his adherents. Vattel accepts the rule but rejects Grotius's application of it to Manlius, while keeping his example of Ulysses and the Cicones.
items.passage: Manlius entreprit donc l'expédition contre les Galates, comme une suite ou un reste de la guerre d'Antiochus.
items.sourcePassage: parce que les Galates & Arioviste ne furent point attaquez comme adhérans à un autre Ennemi, mais comme étant eux-mêmes l'Ennemi principal: or il falloit pour cela, par le Droit des Gens, une nouvelle Déclaration de Guerre

items.question: What impartial conduct must a neutral nation observe?
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 678 holds that a neutral may do nothing at all that could profit one party, and may supply no provisions, arms or anything of any use in war, nor permit enlistment or loans by its subjects. Vattel holds that the neutral must not freely supply troops, arms, munitions or what serves directly to the war, and keeps its freedom to prefer one party in trade and negotiation for the good of the state. Vattel also exempts aid that the neutral is obliged to give.
items.passage: Ne point donner de secours quand on n'y est pas obligé ; ne fournir librement ni troupes, ni armes, ni munitions, ni rien de ce qui sert directement à la guerre.
items.sourcePassage: Qui neutrarum partium esse vult, a bello ita abstinere debet, ut in gratiam belligerantium nihil prorsus faciat, quod parti uni prodesse possit.

items.question: May an ally furnish the aid it owes under an earlier defensive alliance and still remain neutral?
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 736 holds that a state which sends the aid promised under an earlier war alliance cannot be neutral, and that the duty to keep treaties is no excuse. Vattel holds that a sovereign giving the moderate aid owed under an old defensive alliance does not join the war and can otherwise keep exact neutrality. The two give opposite answers on whether treaty aid is compatible with neutrality.
items.passage: il peut donc s'acquitter de ce qu'il doit, et grader du reste une exacte neutralité.
items.sourcePassage: Neutrarum igitur partium esse nequit, si in foedere promissa praestet.

items.question: May a nation conclude a treaty of neutrality, and does necessity excuse it from an alliance obligation?
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 676 holds that a nation may conclude a treaty of neutrality with one belligerent unless it is bound to the other by a war alliance. Vattel holds that very pressing necessity, such as being at the mercy of a far superior enemy, releases a nation even from a perfect obligation under an alliance and permits it to accept neutrality. Vattel adds a necessity exception to the alliance bar that Wolff states without exception.
items.passage: Cette même impuissance me dégageroit même d'une obligation parfaite, contractée par une alliance.
items.sourcePassage: nisi alteri foedere belli obstricta sit

items.question: Which acts (levies, loans, sale of goods) by a neutral are compatible with neutrality?
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 678 holds that a neutral may supply neither party with arms, provisions or anything useful in war, may not permit levies on its territory, and may not let its subjects lend money, since this amounts to giving subsidies. Vattel holds that permitting levies, lending at interest and selling arms and naval stores to one belligerent do not break neutrality when done in the ordinary use of the nation's rights and without design to favour. The point of difference is that Wolff treats any material benefit to one side as aid, while Vattel judges by impartiality and intent.
items.passage: Que le souverain, ou ses sujets prêtent ainsi leur argent à mon ennemi, et qu'ils me le refusent, parce qu'ils n'auront pas la même confiance en moi, ce n'est pas enfreindre la neutralité.
items.sourcePassage: Similiter subditis suis permittere nequit, ut mutuo dent pecunias, cum hoc perinde esse videatur ac dare subsidia.

items.locus: Droit de la guerre et de la paix, Liv. III ch. I § 5
items.question: May neutral nations trade with my enemy, and may I stop that trade?
items.comment: Grotius, DGP III.1.5 holds that those who furnish the enemy with things needed for war may be regarded as belonging to the enemy's party. Vattel holds that neutrals who simply pursue their ordinary trade with the enemy remain neutral and exercise a right, and that only manifest partiality takes them out of neutrality. For Vattel the seizure of war goods carried by neutrals rests on necessity and is not counted as an act of hostility against them. His impartiality test is close to Barbeyrac's note on this section, which follows Cocceius against Grotius.
items.passage: Mais si elles ne font que suivre tout uniment leur commerce, elles ne se déclarent point par là contre mes intérêts : elles exercent un droit que rien ne les oblige de me sacrifier.
items.sourcePassage: A l'égard de la prémiére sorte, il est certain que l'on peut regarder comme du parti de nôtre Ennemi, ceux qui lui fournissent des choses nécessaires pour la Guerre

items.locus: Droit de la guerre et de la paix, Liv. III ch. I § 5
items.question: May contraband carried by neutrals to the enemy be confiscated, or only seized against payment?
items.comment: Grotius, DGP III.1.5 allows goods of double use bound for the enemy to be stopped only under necessity and subject to restitution, and reserves damages or punishment for carriers who knowingly caused harm or who sustain an evidently unjust enemy. Vattel holds that all contraband that can be taken may be confiscated as good prize, on the grounds of deterrence, notification of the war and settled European usage. The difference lies in the sanction and its ground: confiscation for efficacy and by convention replaces seizure with restitution.
items.passage: On prend donc le parti de confisquer toutes les marchandises de contrebande dont on peut se saisir, afin que la crainte de perdre servant de frein à l'avidité du gain, les marchands des pays neutres s'abstiennent d'en porter à l'ennemi.
items.sourcePassage: la nécessité me donne droit alors de m'en saisir, comme nous (c) l'avons expliqué ailleurs, à la charge de restituer, s'il ne survient quelque autre raison qui m'en empêche

items.locus: Droit de la guerre et de la paix, Liv. III ch. I § 5
items.question: May neutrals trade with a besieged or blockaded place, and how may violators be treated?
items.comment: Grotius, DGP III.1.5 makes a neutral who supplies a besieged or blockaded place liable for damages only when the place was about to yield and he could know it, and allows punishment only where the enemy's injustice is evident. Vattel holds that all commerce with a besieged or blockaded place is forbidden and that anyone who tries to enter it or bring anything in without leave may be treated as an enemy. Vattel drops Grotius's conditions of actual harm, knowledge, imminent surrender and evident injustice.
items.passage: Quand je tiens une place assiégée, ou seulement bloquée, je suis en droit d'empêcher que personne n'y entre, & de traiter en ennemi quiconque entreprend d'y entrer sans ma permission, ou d'y porter quoi que ce soit
items.sourcePassage: comme si j'assiégeois une Place, si je tenois un Port bloqué, & que l'Ennemi fût sur le point de se rendre, ou de faire la paix: le tiers sera tenu de me dédommager du préjudice (d) qu'il m'a causé par sa faute

items.question: Must a neutral give both belligerents impartially the ordinary offices of humanity and trade, and may it favour a friend?
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 683 holds that a neutral must favour neither party more than the other and must give the one whatever it gives the other, with departures allowed only by express treaty. Vattel requires impartiality but allows a neutral with particular ties of friendship to grant one belligerent, in matters not belonging to war, the preferences due to friends, and to continue commercial favours stipulated in earlier treaties. Vattel thus admits unequal treatment without any agreement made with reference to the war.
items.passage: ce qui n'empêche point que, si cet état neutre a des relations particulieres d'amitié et de bon voisinage avec l'un de ceux se font la guerre, il ne puisse lui accorder, dans tout ce qui n'appartient pas à la guerre, ces préférences qui sont dues aux amis.
items.sourcePassage: Quod uni praestatur, id praestandum quoque alteri est, si eodem indiget.

items.locus: Droit de la guerre et de la paix, Liv. II ch. II § 13
items.question: When may a nation force a passage through another's territory?
items.comment: Grotius, DGP II.2.13 holds that passage for a just cause is owed, so that one must first ask for it but may force it if the master of the country refuses. Vattel holds that in doubtful cases the owner's judgment on the innocence of the passage prevails and his refusal must be borne even if thought unjust. Vattel allows force only where the innocence of the passage is manifest, which he thinks almost never true of an army, or in extreme necessity. His position moves toward Barbeyrac's note, which makes passage a strict right only in extreme necessity.
items.passage: Dans tous les cas douteux, il faut s'en rapporter au jugement du maître, sur l'innocence de l'usage qu'on demande à faire des choses appartenantes à autrui, (L. II. §§. 128. & 130.) & souffrir son refus, bien qu'on le croye injuste.
items.sourcePassage: L'opinion véritable est ici celle qui tient le milieu, c'est qu'il faut prémiérement (8) demander passage; mais que, si le Maître du Païs le refuse, on peut alors le forcer.

items.locus: Droit de la guerre et de la paix, Liv. II ch. II § 13
items.question: Does fear of the danger of an army's passage justify refusing it?
items.comment: Grotius, DGP II.2.13 holds that fear inspired by the numbers of those asking passage is no ground for refusing it, since that fear takes nothing from their right and precautions such as small detachments, disarming or hostages are available. Vattel, naming Grotius, holds that probable fear founded on good reasons justifies refusing entry to a powerful army when necessity does not require the passage. His ground is that the right of passage is imperfect except in pressing necessity or perfectly evident innocence. Vattel follows Barbeyrac's note, which objects that Grotius assumes the point in question.
items.passage: Quand la nécessité n'exige pas le passage, le seul danger qu'il y a à recevoir chez soi une armée puissante peut autoriser à lui refuser l'entrée du pays.
items.sourcePassage: En vain voudroit-on se dispenser de donner passage, à cause du grand nombre, qui nous fait appréhender quelque chose de la part de ceux qui le demandent.

items.question: Must a neutral treat both belligerents equally regarding passage?
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 684 holds that a neutral is bound to grant both belligerents access and safe passage and must avoid anything that shows greater favour to one than to the other. Vattel requires only that the neutral grant or refuse passage alike to both, and permits different treatment where a change of circumstances furnishes solid reasons. Vattel thus treats passage as within the neutral's discretion and admits an exception to strict parity that Wolff does not.
items.passage: à moins que le changement des circonstances ne lui fournisse de solides raisons d'en user autrement.
items.sourcePassage: cavendum saltem est, ne quid fiat, quod prodit majorem favorem erga partem unam, quam alteram

items.question: Difference between what is truly right in war (only necessary means) and what is merely permitted or unpunished among nations
items.comment: Wolff, Institutiones § 1215 holds that under the voluntary law of nations the effects of war are held just on both sides and that what is necessary to obtain one's right is left to each belligerent's conscience. Vattel holds that nations must keep to general rules, so that a hostile act counts as lawful among nations only when it is recognised as necessary in its generality to overcome resistance, while its unnecessary use remains guilty in conscience. Vattel replaces Wolff's reliance on each belligerent's own judgement of necessity with an external test of generic necessity.
items.passage: dès qu'il est certain et bien reconnu que tel moyen, tel acte d'hostilité est nécessaire dans sa généralité, pour surmonter la résistance de l'ennemi et atteindre le but d'une guerre légitime, ce moyen, pris ainsi en général, passe pour légitime et honnête dans la guerre, suivant le droit des gens
items.sourcePassage: et ideo quoque uniuscujusque conscientiae relinquatur , quid ad consecutionem juris sui necessarium videatur

items.question: Case in which life may be refused to a surrendering enemy (enormous crimes against the law of nations)
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 797 holds that a surrendered enemy may be killed only for his own capital crime, that no one may be punished for another's act, and that a few may not expiate the crime of the whole nation. Vattel holds that a ferocious nation which observes no rules of war may be chastised in the persons of those captured, whom he counts among the guilty. Vattel extends guilt for the nation's conduct to individual captives, which Wolff expressly forbids.
items.passage: on peut la châtier dans la personne de ceux que l'on saisit, ( ils sont du nombre des coupables,)
items.sourcePassage: nulla vero ratio est, cur pauci luant crimen totius civitatis, pro qua eorum vita oppignorata esse nequit

items.question: Reprisals in war: killing prisoners for the enemy's wrongful killing of one's own
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 797 holds that prisoners who have surrendered may not be killed for the wrongs of their ruler, since no one may be punished for the deed of another. Vattel holds that against an inhuman enemy who repeatedly kills prisoners a prince may refuse quarter to some captives and treat them as his own were treated, though he advises against it. Vattel grounds the exception in the right to sacrifice enemy lives to one's own safety, not in punishment, and so escapes Wolff's bar on vicarious punishment.
items.passage: il semble que, s'il a affaire à un ennemi inhumain, qui s'abandonne souvent à de pareils excès, il peut refuser la vie à quelques-uns des prisonniers qu'il fera, et les traiter comme on aura traité les siens
items.sourcePassage: cum nemo puniri possit ob factum alienum

items.locus: Droit de la guerre et de la paix, Liv. III ch. XI § 16
items.question: May the victor put to death a commander for obstinately defending his place?
items.comment: Grotius, DGP III.11.16 holds that obstinate defence of one's party, where the cause of the war is not wholly dishonourable, deserves no punishment or at least is never a capital crime. Vattel agrees in general but allows a governor to be threatened with death, and to suffer it, when his resistance is manifestly useless, as when the rest of the state is conquered and no relief can come. Vattel's exception turns on the uselessness of the resistance, not on the dishonesty of the cause, and he confines it to wars of doubtful justice.
items.passage: La résistance poussée à l'extrêmité, ne devient punissable dans un subalterne, que dans les seules occasions où elle est manifestement inutile : c'est alors opiniâtreté, & non fermeté ou valeur.
items.sourcePassage: Pour ce qui est de l'opiniâtreté à défendre son Parti, si le sujet de la Guerre n'est pas entiérement deshonnête, cela ne mérite aucune punition, comme le représentoient autrefois les Néapolitains, au rapport de (c) PROCOPE; ou du moins ce n'est pas un crime digne de mort.

items.question: May prisoners who cannot be kept or fed be killed, or released on parole, and how far do parole engagements bind?
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 818 holds that the captor may release prisoners on whatever condition he wishes and that their own nation cannot prevent them from keeping their promises. Vattel holds that such conventions are bounded by the sovereign's rights over his subjects. A captor may bind released prisoners not to fight until the end of the war, but he may not require them to renounce for ever the liberty of fighting for their country.
items.passage: mais il n'a point le droit d'exiger qu'ils renoncent pour toujours à la liberté de combattre pour leur patrie
items.sourcePassage: eos dimittere potest ea lege, qua voluerit, et quod hi promittunt, dum dimittuntur, servare tenentur

items.locus: Droit de la guerre et de la paix, Liv. III ch. XXI § 24
items.question: Is the state obliged to ransom its captured soldiers, and may it lawfully forbid their ransom?
items.comment: Grotius, DGP III.21.24 holds that a law forbidding the ransom of prisoners of war is unjust unless experience shows such rigour necessary to prevent greater or more numerous evils, in which case charity obliges the prisoners to bear their lot. Vattel holds that any nation may, like the Romans, enact such a law to spur its soldiers to the most vigorous resistance, and that once the whole society has agreed to it no one can complain, though the law is very harsh. Grotius makes the justice of the law depend on proven necessity and censures the Roman practice; Vattel rests it on the consent of the society and a purpose of military discipline, with no test of necessity.
items.passage: Cependant il faut convenir que toute nation peut, à l'exemple des Romains, & pour exciter les soldats à la plus vigoureuse résistance, faire une loi qui défende de racheter jamais les prisonniers de guerre.
items.sourcePassage: On ne sauroit donc, à mon avis, regarder comme juste une Loi, qui défend de racheter les Prisonniers de Guerre; à moins que l'expérience ne fasse voir, qu'il est besoin d'une telle rigueur, pour prévenir des maux plus grands, ou en plus grand nombre, qui sans cela sont inévitables moralement parlant.

items.question: May an enemy be assassinated or poisoned?
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 882 holds that killing an enemy by a hired assassin is not unlawful by nature, since deceit is lawful in war and payment does not change the act. Vattel separates permitted surprises from assassination, defined as killing by treachery through traitors or disguised emissaries. He declares such assassination infamous and execrable in both the agent and the one who orders it.
items.passage: je dis qu'un pareil attentat est une action infame et exécrable, dans celui qui l'exécute, et dans celui qui la commande
items.sourcePassage: hostem interficere immisso percussore naturaliter illicitum non est

items.question: May an enemy be assassinated or poisoned?
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 877 holds that killing an enemy by poison is permitted by natural law, since it makes no difference whether he is removed by sword or by poison, and he treats abstention as mere generosity. Vattel holds that poisoning is contrary to the laws of war and forbidden by both natural law and the consent of civilised peoples. Vattel rests the prohibition on the ruinous effect such a practice would have on human society.
items.passage: L'assassinat et l'empoisonnement sont donc contraires aux loix de la guerre, également proscrits par la loi naturelle et par le consentement des peuples civilisés.
items.sourcePassage: Naturaliter hostem veneno interimere licet.

items.locus: Droit de la guerre et de la paix, Liv. III ch. IV § 15
items.question: May one lawfully have an enemy assassinated or poisoned?
items.comment: Grotius, DGP III.4.15 holds that by the law of nature it makes no difference whether an enemy who may lawfully be killed is killed by the sword or by poison, and that poison is forbidden only by the voluntary law of nations resting on the consent of the more civilised peoples. Vattel rejects as a strange maxim the view that the manner of killing is indifferent and holds assassination and poisoning to be forbidden by natural law itself, because the practice would be ruinous to human society, as well as by the consent of civilised peoples. The point of difference is the ground of the prohibition. For Vattel the sovereign who uses poison or assassins breaks natural law and becomes an enemy of mankind whom all nations may unite to punish.
items.passage: L'assassinat & l'empoisonnement sont donc contraires aux loix de la guerre, également proscrits par la loi naturelle & par le consentement des peuples civilisés.
items.sourcePassage: Par exemple, lors qu'il est permis de tuer quelcun, il n'importe, à considérer le Droit de Nature, qu'on se serve pour cela de l'Epée, ou du Poison.

items.question: May poisoned weapons be used?
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 878 holds that poisoned bullets and arrows are not unlawful by nature, since what makes killing the enemy lawful also makes the poison lawful. Vattel holds that poisoned weapons are forbidden by natural law, which does not allow the evils of war to be extended without limit. Vattel argues that an enemy put out of combat need not die of his wounds, where Wolff treats a double mortal wound as indifferent.
items.passage: Mais cet usage n'en est pas moins interdit par la loi naturelle, qui ne permet point d'étendre à l'infini les maux de la guerre.
items.sourcePassage: globis vel sagittis venenatis in bello uti, illicitum naturaliter non est

items.question: Is poisoning wells and springs forbidden, and on what ground?
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 879 forbids poisoning springs because the water is common and the poison would kill people who may not lawfully be killed in war. Vattel also condemns it but denies that harm to innocents is the true ground, since an enemy ship is fired on even with neutral passengers aboard. The rule is shared and its ground is changed, with the prohibition resting on the ban on poison itself.
items.passage: C'est une raison de plus ; mais ce n'est ni la seule, ni même la véritable : car on ne laisse pas de tirer sur un vaisseau ennemi, quoiqu'il ait à bord des passagers neutres.
items.sourcePassage: Ast si fontes veneno inficiantur, non ita intendi potest hostis interemtio, ut non interitus immineat inde etiam iis, quos jure belli interficere minime licet.

items.question: When and how may an enemy be punished by taking his property?
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 581 holds that a nation which has done injury may be punished by the loss of corporeal and incorporeal things, and by arms if security cannot otherwise be had, the right of punishing being unlimited. Vattel holds that not every war gives a just ground for punishment. Only manifest injustice without plausible pretext, or odious excess in conduct, gives the victor a right to punish, and an enemy in a doubtful cause is presumed to act in good faith.
items.passage: Ce n'est donc que l'injustice manifeste, dénuée même de prétextes plausibles ou d'odieux excès dans les procédés, qui donnent à un ennemi le droit de punir.
items.sourcePassage: In poenam Genti adimi possunt res tam corporales, quam incorporales, veluti jura ad certos actus in territorio laesae: immo licite quoque sumuntur arma in laedentem, nisi aliter securitati prospici possit.

items.question: When may a country be ravaged and burned?
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 825 holds that destroying towns and villages is lawful as punishment for a particular delict, whether of the inhabitants or of the sovereign, since the sovereign's act is imputed to the whole nation. Vattel condemns ravaging a country to punish only the sovereign through an innocent people. He admits devastation to chastise a ferocious nation and adds a non-penal ground, the making of a barrier to cover one's frontier.
items.passage: Qu'il est cruel de la faire parvenir jusqu'à lui par la désolation d'un peuple innocent !
items.sourcePassage: Dico singulare praecedere debere delictum, non modo eorum, qui urbes, oppida et pagos incolunt, verum etiam summae potestatis, cum qua bellum est

items.question: Which buildings must be spared when ravaging a country?
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 824 permits the destruction of fields, buildings, gardens and vineyards whenever camp, siege or battle require it, and holds that no distinction or quality of things counts. Vattel holds that, whatever the ground of ravaging, buildings that honour humanity and add nothing to the enemy's strength must be spared, and that their destruction is excused only by war operations and condemned when the camp could have been placed elsewhere. Vattel makes the quality of the object a limit that Wolff expressly excludes.
items.passage: on doit épargner les édifices qui font honneur à l'humanité, et qui necontribuent point à rendre l'ennemi plus puissant
items.sourcePassage: Nulla hic valet distinctio rerum, qualiscunque tandem ea sit, nec earundem attenduntur qualitates

items.question: What does the voluntary law of nations tolerate regarding excessive hostilities?
items.comment: Wolff, Institutiones § 1215 grounds the voluntary law of war in the equal treatment of both belligerents and leaves to each one's conscience what seems necessary to obtain its right. Vattel accepts the toleration but holds that the voluntary law itself condemns every hostility that by its nature does nothing for the success of arms, such as the deliberate destruction of monuments, and acts evidently without necessity. Vattel sets an external limit where Wolff refers the matter wholly to conscience.
items.passage: condamne toute hostilité qui, de sa nature et indépendamment des circonstances, ne fait rien au succès de nos armes, n'augmente point nos forces, et n'affoiblit point l'ennemi
items.sourcePassage: et ideo quoque uniuscujusque conscientiae relinquatur , quid ad consecutionem juris sui necessarium videatur

items.locus: Droit de la guerre et de la paix, Liv. III ch. IV § 4
items.question: How far does the voluntary law of nations tolerate excess in hostilities against enemy property, and what does it condemn absolutely?
items.comment: Grotius, DGP III.4.4 holds that the law of nations grants impunity for acts of hostility because outsiders cannot know how far necessity required them, and leaves the measure of hostility wholly to the conscience of the belligerents. Vattel gives the same reason for tolerating excess but holds that the voluntary law of nations still condemns every hostility that by its nature does nothing for the success of arms, such as the deliberate destruction of temples, tombs and public monuments, and any excess whose needlessness is fully evident. The difference is that Vattel sets an external limit, judged by the nature of the act, within the voluntary law itself, where Grotius leaves the whole matter to conscience.
