items.passage: condamne toute hostilité qui, de sa nature & indépendamment des circonstances, ne fait rien au succès de nos armes, n'augmente point nos forces, & n'affoiblit point l'ennemi
items.sourcePassage: Ainsi il vaut mieux certainement laisser tout cela à la conscience de ceux qui sont en Guerre, que d'en faire juges les autres.

items.question: Are stratagems and ruses of war lawful, and what limits them?
items.comment: Wolff, Institutiones § 1203 holds deceit lawful in war whenever it obtains what open force could obtain, with the sole limit that it may not lie within promissory speech. Vattel adds that stratagems must respect the rights of humanity as well as good faith and must avoid practices whose introduction would harm mankind. The additional limit is humanity, though Vattel's example of false distress signals is also reduced to perfidy.
items.passage: Il faut respecter, dans l'usage des stratagêmes, non seulement la foi qui est due à l'ennemi, mais encore les droits de l'humanité, et prendre garde de ne point faire des choses dont l'introduction seroit préjudiciable au genre humain
items.sourcePassage: si dolo idem consequi datur , quod vi aperta licebat , quin is in bello licitus sit, utpote minus nocumentum afferens vi aperta, dubitandum non est

items.locus: Droit de la guerre et de la paix, Liv. III ch. I § 20
items.question: Which stratagems and ruses of war are legitimate (excluding perfidy), and were the peoples who refused them right?
items.comment: Grotius, DGP III.1.20 holds that peoples who refused naturally permitted deceits acted from extraordinary greatness of soul, and that Christians ought to follow that maxim because simplicity is commanded them and they may not lie even to an enemy. Vattel holds that ruses free of perfidy are legitimate and, where they spare blood, more praiseworthy than a murderous siege or battle, and that the peoples who scorned stratagems showed more generosity than wisdom. Grotius ranks abstention from deceit as the higher course and urges it on Christians; Vattel ranks the surest lawful means as the most praiseworthy and prefers open force only on the prudential ground that it gives a more lasting advantage.
items.passage: Il y avoit plus de générosité que de sagesse dans une pareille conduite.
items.sourcePassage: Les (6) Chrétiens doivent suivre cette maxime, d'autant plus que la (a) simplicité leur est non seulement commandée, mais encore qu'il leur est défendu de (b) dire des paroles (7) vaines; & qu'ils ont à imiter l'exemple de celui (c) en la bouche duquel on n'a point remarqué de tromperie.

items.question: Is the use of spies in war lawful?
items.comment: Wolff, Institutiones § 1208 holds that sending spies is lawful and gives the right to punish them to the party whose arms are just. Vattel holds that spies are justly put to death because there is no other protection against them, and that a sovereign may not in general require this service of his subjects. Vattel grounds punishment in self-protection rather than in the justice of the cause and adds a limit on the sovereign's power to command espionage.
items.passage: Le souverain n'est donc pas en droit d'exiger un pareil service de ses sujets, si ce n'est peut - être dans quelque cas singulier, et de la plus grande importance.
items.sourcePassage: Ast cum noceant ei, ad quem mittuntur, is, cujus arma justa sunt, habet jus eosdem puniendi.

items.locus: Droit de la guerre et de la paix, Liv. III ch. IV § 18
items.question: May spies be used and punished, and may a sovereign demand spying of his subjects?
items.comment: Grotius, DGP III.4.18 holds that the law of nations permits sending spies and that a captured spy may be treated with great rigour, justly if the war is waged for a manifestly lawful cause and otherwise only with impunity by the right of war. Vattel holds that spies are justly put to death because there is hardly any other means of guarding against the harm they do. Grotius ties the justice of the penalty to the justice of the war; Vattel grounds it in the necessity of self-protection, which holds for either belligerent.
items.passage: On punit communément les espions du dernier supplice, & cela avec justice, puisque l'on n'a guere d'autre moyen de se garantir du mal qu'ils peuvent faire
items.sourcePassage: & cela justement, si on fait la Guerre pour un sujet manifestement légitime; toûjours impunément, & par droit de Guerre

items.question: What is the author of an unjust war bound to render?
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 789 holds that the author of an unjust war is liable to punishment for every hostility he commits, because each is an injury, the penalty taking the form of a pecuniary prestation. Vattel holds that the author of an unjust war owes reparation or satisfaction, and punishment only when it is necessary for example and for the safety of the injured party and of human society. Vattel makes punishment conditional on necessity where Wolff derives it directly from the injury.
items.passage: et même à la peine, si la peine est nécessaire pour l'exemple, pour la sûreté de l'offensé, et pour celle de la société humaine
items.sourcePassage: Qui bellum injustum gerit, ob hostilitates, quas committit, tenetur alteri in poenam.

items.locus: Droit de la guerre et de la paix, Liv. I ch. I § 14
items.question: Does the voluntary law of nations give the unjust belligerent only external impunity, and on what is that law founded (natural law vs consent)?
items.comment: Grotius, DGP I.1.14 defines the law of nations as a human law that has acquired binding force from the will of all peoples or of many, proved like unwritten civil law by constant practice. Vattel holds that the voluntary law of nations rests not on the actual consent of peoples but on natural law, which obliges nations to consent and supplies a consent they are not free to withhold; a consent proved from history would only be conventional law binding those who gave it. Vattel follows Barbeyrac's note in denying that the consent of peoples founds this law, while rejecting Barbeyrac's conclusion that a law of nations distinct from natural law is a chimera.
items.passage: ce que nous appellons droit des gens volontaire, consiste dans des regles de conduite, de droit externe, auxquelles la loi naturelle oblige les nations de consentir
items.sourcePassage: ce qui a aquis force d'obliger par (3) un effet de la volonté de tous les Peuples, ou du moins (4) de plusieurs

items.question: When does conquered immovable property (lands, cities, provinces) definitively pass to the conqueror?
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 863 holds that occupying cities and lands occupies the sovereignty over them in the same act, once resistance ceases. Vattel holds that conquered immovables pass into the conqueror's power on seizure, but that the acquisition is consummated only by the treaty of peace or by the entire subjection and extinction of the former state. Vattel separates possession by arms from a perfected title.
items.passage: mais l'acquisition ne se consomme, la propiété ne devient stable et parfaite , que par le traité de paix , ou par l'entiere soumission et l'extinction de l'état auquel ces villes et provinces appartenoient
items.sourcePassage: consequenter urbibus ac terris occupatis imperium simul occupatum est

items.question: What rights does a conqueror acquire over a conquered city or province?
items.comment: Wolff, Institutiones § 1205 holds that the conqueror acquires sovereignty as it exists in the people and, absent a pact, may change the form of the commonwealth at will. Vattel holds that the conqueror acquires only the rights the dispossessed sovereign held, with all their limitations, so that the conquered keep their privileges unless forfeited by crime or by taking up arms. The measure of the conquest is the former ruler's title in Vattel and the people's original sovereignty in Wolff.
items.passage: ne speut y acquérir justement que les mêmes droits qu'y possédoit le souverain contre lequel il a pris lesarmes
items.sourcePassage: Quamobrem si sine pactione imperium acquirit victor , formam Reip. pro lubitu mutare potest et de modo habendi imperium itidem pro lubitu disponere.

items.question: What may a conqueror do with a wholly conquered state and its people?
items.comment: Wolff, Institutiones § 1205 holds that a victor who acquires sovereignty without a pact acquires it as it exists in the people and may change the form of the state and the manner of ruling at will. Vattel holds that a conqueror whose quarrel is only with the sovereign acquires no more than the rights of the deposed sovereign and must govern by the laws of the state once the people submit. Wolff's victor holds the people's original sovereignty, while Vattel's victor steps into the limited rights of the former ruler.
items.passage: S'il n'a à se plaindre que du souverain, la raison nous démontre qu'il n'acquiert par sa conquête que les droits qui appartenoient réellement à ce souverain dépossédé ; et aussi-tôt que le peuple se soumet , il doit le gouverner suivant les loix de l'état.
items.sourcePassage: Quamobrem si sine pactione imperium acquirit victor , formam Reip. pro lubitu mutare potest et de modo habendi imperium itidem pro lubitu disponere.

items.locus: Droit de la guerre et de la paix, Liv. III ch. VIII § 1
items.question: What may a conqueror do with an entire conquered state or nation (limits of his right over the vanquished)?
items.comment: Grotius, DGP III.8.1 holds that, as individual captives may be enslaved, a victor may impose on a whole conquered people a civil, a purely despotic or a mixed subjection, and may alienate a sovereignty that resided in the people. Vattel calls the conqueror's absolute mastery a monstrous principle and derives all his right from just self-defence, which allows reparation, punishment and a rigour that must end once danger ceases, but no enslavement of a submitted people. Vattel follows Barbeyrac's note in holding that a subjection the vanquished do not accept leaves the state of war in being.
items.passage: Lorsqu'un souverain, se prétendant le maître absolu de la destinée d'un peuple qu'il a vaincu , veut le réduire en esclavage, il fait subsister l'état de guerre entre ce peuple & lui.
items.sourcePassage: imposer à tout le Corps des Ennemis, soit qu'il fasse un Etat entier, ou seulement partie de l'Etat, une Sujettion ou purement civile, ou purement despotique, ou qui tienne de l'une & de l'autre

items.locus: Droit de la guerre et de la paix, Liv. III ch. IX § 6
items.question: Does postliminium restore to a retaken town (or private owners) goods alienated by the enemy while he held it?
items.comment: Grotius, DGP III.9.6 holds that a captor acquires by the right of war a conditional ownership of his prisoner's goods lying in neutral countries; if he alienates them, goods capable of postliminium pass only at the buyer's risk and revert to the returning prisoner, while other goods pass outright. Vattel declares the question void, because the captor gains only a right to hold the prisoner until peace or ransom and acquires no right over goods he has not seized. Vattel reaches the result of Barbeyrac's note, that the prisoner recovers all such goods, on the different ground that captivity gives the captor no property in the prisoner or his goods.
items.passage: car le souverain qui fait un prisonnier à la guerre , n'a d'autre droit que celui de le retenir jusqu'à la fin de la guerre, ou jusqu'à ce-qu'il soit racheté ( §§. 148 & suiv. ) ; & il n'en acquiert aucun sur ses biens, sinon en tant qu'il peut s'en saisir.
items.sourcePassage: Ainsi le droit de Propriété qu'avoit sur les biens du Prisonnier celui qui le possedoit par droit de Guerre, n'étoit pas un droit absolu, mais un droit conditionel

items.question: Does marriage survive a spouse's captivity?
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 908 holds without condition that captivity does not dissolve marriage, since captives keep their rights, and that the wife may not remarry while there is hope of return. Vattel holds that the bond survives captivity among nations that have made marriage indissoluble or lifelong unless dissolved by a judge. Vattel makes the rule depend on each nation's marriage law and drops Wolff's bar on the wife's remarriage.
items.passage: Chez les nations qui ont rendu le mariage indissoluble , ou qui l'établissent pour la vie, à moins qu'il ne soitdissous par le juge, le lien subsiste, malgré la captivité de l'un des conjoints
items.sourcePassage: per captivitatem matrimonium non dissolvitur

items.question: What force have civil laws, treaties and customs on postliminium?
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 907 holds that what custom or pact has introduced on postliminium between certain nations counts between them as customary or pactitious law. Vattel holds that such customs bind only when they contain nothing contrary to natural law, and that customs which violate it are void and must be abolished. Vattel attaches to customary postliminium a natural-law validity condition that Wolff's section does not state.
items.passage: Mais celles qui donnent atteinte à cette loi sacrée, sont vicieuses et sans force.
items.sourcePassage: quae vero inter certas Gentes moribus introducta, vel pactionibus determinata sunt, ea inter illas Gentes pro jure consuetudinario, vel pactitio habenda

items.locus: Droit de la guerre et de la paix, Liv. III ch. XVIII § 1
items.question: May subjects commit acts of hostility without the sovereign's order?
items.comment: Grotius, DGP III.18.1, holds that by natural law and true justice any person may act against the enemy in a just war, and that the ban on private hostilities rests only on civil law and military discipline. Vattel grounds the ban in the sovereign's exclusive right to make war and to direct its operations, and admits only self-defence as an exception. Vattel follows Barbeyrac's note against Grotius, which derives the ban from natural law and from the subject's engagements to the sovereign.
items.passage: Les sujets ne peuvent donc agir ici d'eux - mêmes, & il ne leur est pas permis de commettre aucune hostilité, sans ordre du souverain.
items.sourcePassage: C'est donc en vertu du Droit Civil, ou des Loix de la Discipline Militaire, qu'il est défendu à toute personne d'agir contre l'Ennemi, sans un ordre du Souverain, ou de ses Ministres.

items.locus: Droit de la guerre et de la paix, Liv. III ch. XVIII § 2
items.question: Do privateers acquire the booty, how far may subjects serve in conscience, and what of foreigners taking commissions?
items.comment: Grotius, DGP III.18.2, holds that privateers who fit out ships at their own cost acquire in true justice only so much of their captures as answers to the debt owed to the state, an equitable arbiter judging whether they have exceeded it. Vattel holds that privateers acquire the booty as a reward for their outlay and risk, by the sovereign's concession and in the measure fixed by their contract. Vattel drops the limit set by the debt and places the subject's question of conscience in the justice of the war, which he may serve unless it is evidently unjust.
items.passage: Les armateurs, qui équippent à leurs frais des vaisseaux pour aller en course, acquierent la propriété du butin, en récompense de leurs avances & des périls qu'ils courent ; & ils l'acquierent par la concession du souverain, qui leur délivre des commissions.
items.sourcePassage: ce n'est que jusqu'à la concurrence de la dette, qu'on aquiert la propriété de ce que l'on prend sur les Ennemis, coupables ou non

items.locus: Droit de la guerre et de la paix, Liv. III ch. XX § 8
items.question: Must the state compensate subjects for losses suffered in war?
items.comment: Grotius, DGP III.20.8, rejects the view that the state owes no compensation for losses caused by hostilities, since the members of one state must bear in common the damage that falls on some of them, though civil law may deny an action. Vattel holds that the state must pay for damage it causes freely by way of precaution, and that losses caused by necessity or by the enemy give no action against the state. He rests this on the presumed intention of those who formed the society and leaves only an equitable duty of relief.
items.passage: on n'a point d'action contre l'état, pour des malheurs de cette nature, pour des pertes qu'il n'a pointcausées librement, mais par nécessité & par accident, en usant de ses droits.
items.sourcePassage: il ne s'étend point jusqu'aux Membres d'un même Etat, dont l'association demande qu'ils supportent en commun (1) les dommages (d) qui arrivent aux uns ou aux autres en conséquence de la communauté où ils sont entrez.

items.question: Who has authority to conclude truces (general vs particular, sovereign vs commander)
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 932 holds that general truces belong to the sovereign alone and that supreme commanders may conclude particular truces within their function when present circumstances make them necessary. Vattel holds that a general's presumed power covers short particular truces whenever they only spare blood, but that a particular truce for a long term requires the sovereign's ratification. Vattel widens the ground from necessity to common advantage and adds a duration limit that Wolff does not draw.
items.passage: Une treve même particuliere, mais pour un long tems, semble encore passer le pouvoir ordinaire d'un général ; il ne peut la conclure que sous réserve de la ratification.
items.sourcePassage: particulares intra limites functionis a summis ducibus possunt, ubi eas necessarias faciunt circumstantiae praesentes

items.locus: Droit de la guerre et de la paix, Liv. III ch. XXII § 8
items.question: Who has authority to conclude truces and similar wartime accords (sovereign or commanders)?
items.comment: Grotius, DGP III.22.8, holds that generals, and even their lieutenants and subordinate officers, may grant a truce binding themselves and their own troops, without distinction of scope or length. Vattel reserves a general truce to the sovereign or to one expressly empowered, requires ratification for a particular truce of long duration, and leaves to commanders only short particular truces. Vattel follows Barbeyrac's note against Grotius, which on Pufendorf's authority excepts general truces and truces of considerable length from the general's power.
items.passage: Suivant cette regle, la treve générale ne peut être conclue & arrêtée que par le souverain lui-même, ou par celui à qui il en a expressément donné le pouvoir.
items.sourcePassage: MAIS pour ce qui est d'accorder quelque (1) Trêve, les Généraux d'armée (a) le peuvent; & même leurs Lieutenans ou Officiers Subalternes

items.locus: Droit de la guerre et de la paix, Liv. III ch. XXI § 5
items.question: From when does a truce bind the contracting parties and their subjects, and who bears the consequences of hostilities committed in ignorance of it?
items.comment: Grotius, DGP III.21.5, holds that subjects are not punishable for hostilities committed before a truce was notified to them, and that the contracting powers must indemnify those who suffered from such acts in the interval. Vattel requires the sovereign only to restore captures made after the truce should have begun, and declares that neither the subjects nor their sovereign owe any indemnity for damage done in blameless ignorance. Vattel imposes a duty to repair damage only where ignorance of the publication is due to fault, against Grotius's rule and Barbeyrac's defence of it.
items.passage: Les sujets qui ne l'ont pas observée, faute de la connoître, ne sont tenus à aucun dédommagement, non plus que leur souverain, qui n'a pu la leur notifier plutôt.
items.sourcePassage: Ce qui n'empêche pas, que les Puissances qui ont conclu ensemble la Trêve (2) ne doivent dédommager (3) ceux qui ont souffert par les actes d'hostilité exercez dans cet intervalle.

items.question: How the time of a truce is reckoned (start, end, day)
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 920 holds that a truce made until a certain day ends at dawn of that day, so the terminal day is excluded, and that a term of days runs from the moment the contract is perfected. Vattel holds that the terminal day should probably be included, since truce is a favourable matter, and that a truce with no fixed start runs only from its first publication. The two give opposite answers on the terminal day and different starting points for the reckoning.
items.passage: comme la treve, qui épargne le sang humain, est sans-doute une matiere favorable, le plus sûr est peut-être d'y comprendre le jour même du terme
items.sourcePassage: Die igitur illucescente, ad quem induciae pactae sunt, eaedem finiuntur.

items.locus: Droit de la guerre et de la paix, Liv. III ch. XXI § 4
items.question: How to fix and count the beginning and end of a truce (inclusive/exclusive days, natural days, start without stated term)
items.comment: Grotius, DGP III.21.4, holds that a day named as the point from which a period of truce is to run is not included in the period, because the preposition 'depuis' separates the term from what follows. Vattel holds that a truce agreed 'depuis le premier de mars' indubitably includes that day, hostilities ceasing on it. Vattel follows Barbeyrac's note against Grotius, which on the authority of Pufendorf and Strauchius rejects the exclusion as inconsistent with the favourable character of a truce.
items.passage: A l'égard du premier de ces deux jours, il paroît indubitable qu'il est compris dans la treve ; car si l'on convient qu'il y aura treve depuis le premier de mars, cela veut dire naturellement, que les hostilités cesseront le premier de mars.
items.sourcePassage: Mais quand on a marqué un Jour, depuis lequel un certain espace de tems commenceroit, ce Jour n'est point compris dans l'espace déterminé

items.locus: Droit de la guerre et de la paix, Liv. III ch. XXI § 7
items.question: What a party may do within its own territory during a truce (general rule)
items.comment: Grotius, DGP III.21.7, holds that withdrawing an army inland, repairing breaches in one's fortifications and levying troops do not breach a truce unless a special article forbids them. Vattel derives the same permissions from the rule that each party may do at home whatever it could do in full peace, and confines the repair of fortifications to a place not actually under siege. The qualification removes the besieged place from a permission that Grotius gives without exception.
items.passage: Ainsi la treve n'empêche point qu'un prince ne puisse lever des soldats, assembler une armée dans ses états, y faire marcher des troupes, y appeller même des auxiliaires, réparer les fortifications d'une place qui n'est point actuellement assiégée.
items.sourcePassage: il n'y a rien là de contraire à la Trêve: non plus que si l'on répare les brêches faites à ses Fortifications, ou si l'on léve des Troupes

items.question: May a besieged governor or besieger continue siege works and repairs during a truce?
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 928 holds that during a truce nothing serving the defence of a besieged town may be done and that everything must remain on both sides in the state it was in when the truce began. Vattel bars the governor from repairing breaches or raising new fortifications but allows him to continue interior works that the enemy's attacks and fire would not have prevented. Vattel replaces Wolff's standstill rule with a test of what the truce adds to either side's capacity.
items.passage: la cessation d'armes n'empêche point le gouverneur de continuer, dans l'intérieur de sa place, des travaux auxquels les attaques et le feu de l'ennemi n'étoient pas un obstacle
items.sourcePassage: omnia ex utraque parte manere debent in eodem statu, in quo sunt eo ipso momento, quo induciae incipiunt

items.question: May a besieged governor or besieger continue siege works and repairs during a truce?
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 927 holds that during a truce one must abstain from every act serving to take or to defend a besieged town. Vattel allows the governor to continue interior works that enemy fire would not have hindered. Vattel exempts a class of defensive works that Wolff's general prohibition covers.
items.passage: la cessation d'armes n'empêche point le gouverneur de continuer, dans l'intérieur de sa place, des travaux auxquels les attaques et le feu de l'ennemi n'étoient pas un obstacle
items.sourcePassage: ab omni actu abstinendum, qui ad urbem obsessam occupandam, vel ex parte altera ad eandem defendendam facit

items.locus: Droit de la guerre et de la paix, Liv. III ch. XXI § 10
items.question: May a governor bring in relief during an armistice made for a particular object (burying the dead)?
items.comment: Grotius, DGP III.21.10, holds that during a truce granted only to bury the dead nothing new may be undertaken that changes the state of things, and he denies a besieged town relief or provisions during a truce granted to shelter it from attack. Vattel reads a burial armistice by its object alone: works that the suspended fire would have prevented are barred, but the governor may quietly bring relief in at a point far from the attack. Vattel's ground, that the besieger must blame his own lack of vigilance, is the argument of Pufendorf that Barbeyrac's note rejects in favour of Grotius.
items.passage: Mais rien n'empêche que, pendant une suspension d'armes de cette nature, le gouverneur ne fasse entrer sans bruit quelque secours, par un endroit éloigné de l'attaque.
items.sourcePassage: Si l'on a, par exemple, accordé une Trêve seulement pour enterrer les Morts, on ne doit rien entreprendre de nouveau, qui apporte aucun changement à l'état des choses (1) pendant ce court intervalle.

items.question: May an army withdraw or advance during a truce, particularly one for burying the dead?
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 927 holds that during a truce a party may do what it likes within its own uncontested borders, including withdrawing its army, but may do nothing outside them that worsens the enemy's condition. Vattel holds that an army under a truce for burying the dead may not leave its defile in view of the enemy, yet may withdraw quietly by its rear without breaking faith. Wolff draws the line by territory and by harm to the enemy, while Vattel draws it by the object of the truce and the use of the agreement as a trap.
items.passage: Mais si cette armée défile sans bruit par ses derrieres, et se met en lieu de sûreté, elle n'aura rien fait contre la parole donnée.
items.sourcePassage: ast cum extra eosdem nil facere liceat, quo hostis conditio deterior redditur

items.locus: Droit de la guerre et de la paix, Liv. III ch. XXI § 10
items.question: May an army use an armistice for a particular object (burying the dead) to withdraw from a bad position?
items.comment: Grotius, DGP III.21.10, holds that during a truce granted only to bury the dead nothing new may be undertaken that changes the state of things. Vattel holds that a burial armistice binds the parties only not to attack each other while the dead are buried, so an army that files off quietly by its rear to a place of safety breaks no promise, and proposing such an armistice to cover a retreat is an innocent stratagem. Barbeyrac's note to Grotius names withdrawal to a safer post as one of the acts this truce forbids.
items.passage: Mais si cette armée défile sans bruit par ses derrieres, & se met en lieu de sûreté, elle n'aura rien fait contre la parole donnée.
items.sourcePassage: Si l'on a, par exemple, accordé une Trêve seulement pour enterrer les Morts, on ne doit rien entreprendre de nouveau, qui apporte aucun changement à l'état des choses (1) pendant ce court intervalle.

items.locus: Droit de la guerre et de la paix, Liv. III ch. XXI § 7
items.question: May an army use an armistice for a particular object (burying the dead) to withdraw from a bad position?
items.comment: Grotius, DGP III.21.7, holds that withdrawing one's army further into one's own territory is not contrary to a truce unless a special article forbids it. Vattel allows an army that has concluded an armistice to bury the dead to file off quietly by its rear, but forbids it to march out of its defiles in sight of the enemy, who may lawfully repulse it. Vattel makes the lawfulness of the retreat depend on whether the army uses the armistice to do what it could not have done under hostilities.
items.passage: De même, si une armée, engagée dans un mauvais pas, propose & conclut un armistice pour enterrer les morts après un combat, elle ne pourra, pendant la suspension d'armes, sortir de ses défilés à la vue de l'ennemi, & se retirer impunément.
items.sourcePassage: POUR ce qui est de se retirer plus avant dans ses Etats avec son Armée, comme le fit autrefois Philippe, au rapport de (a) TITE LIVE; il n'y a rien là de contraire à la Trêve

items.question: May enemy subjects/garrisons be incited to revolt, and deserters received, during a truce?
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 923 holds that during a truce it is not lawful to receive enemy subjects who wish to defect, since nothing touching the enemy may be altered while the truce lasts. Vattel holds that deserters and transfugees may be received during a truce, as they may be even in peace absent a treaty forbidding it. Both forbid soliciting garrisons and inciting revolt. They give opposite answers on the reception of defectors.
items.passage: Pour ce qui est des déserteurs et des transfuges, on peut les recevoir pendant la treve
items.sourcePassage: Induciarum tempore subditos deficere ad hostem volentes recipere non licet

items.question: What of those held by an insuperable obstacle in enemy territory when a truce expires?
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 929 holds that persons kept in enemy territory by force majeure when a truce expires have no right to return and may be held captive, and he expressly denies them the delay owed to foreigners at the outbreak of war. Vattel grants the same strict right but holds that humanity and generosity ordinarily require a sufficient delay for withdrawal. The difference is an added duty of humanity that Wolff's reasoning excludes.
items.passage: Mais l'humanité et la générofité demandent pour l'ordinaire, qu'on leur donne un délai suffisant pour se retirer.
items.sourcePassage: quascunque personas hostiles intra terras suas deprehensas captivas detinere, consequenter eaedem jus redeundi non habent

items.locus: Droit de la guerre et de la paix, Liv. III ch. XXI § 9
items.question: What is the position of persons held back by an insurmountable obstacle in enemy territory after the truce has expired?
items.comment: Grotius, DGP III.21.9, holds that persons kept in enemy territory past the end of a truce by an unforeseen and insurmountable accident may be held as prisoners of war, because their detention is not a penalty that the accident could excuse but the use of a right of war only suspended for a time. Vattel reaches the same strict rule on the ground that the accident was one they could foresee and to which they chose to expose themselves. Grotius makes the foreseeability of the accident irrelevant to the right, while Vattel rests the right on the travellers' acceptance of the risk.
items.passage: C'est un accident qu'ils pouvoient prévoir, & auquel ils ont bien voulu s'exposer.
items.sourcePassage: Car dans ces exemples il s'agit d'une punition, dont l'accident imprévû & inévitable met à couvert; au lieu que, dans le cas dont nous traitons, il n'y a point proprement de peine, mais seulement l'usage d'un droit, qui n'étoit suspendu que pour un certain tems.

items.question: Does war resume at truce expiry without a new declaration?
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 916 holds that no new declaration is needed when a truce ends and that one would be made without any reason. Vattel accepts that no declaration is required but holds that after a long truce it is fitting to make a declaration before resuming arms, citing the Roman fetials at Veii. Vattel supplies a reason of moderation for the act Wolff calls groundless.
items.passage: de ne point reprendre les armes à la fin d'une treve qui en avoit fait disparoître et oublier tout l'appareil, sans faire quelque déclaration
items.sourcePassage: Nova igitur denunciatio absque ulla ratione fieret.

items.locus: Droit de la guerre et de la paix, Liv. III ch. XXIII § 5
items.question: Are promises made to the enemy by private individuals (soldiers, subjects) valid?
items.comment: Grotius, DGP III.23.5, holds that a private person may validly bind himself to the enemy concerning his own person and goods, because a convention that avoids a greater evil counts as advantageous and no duty to the state voids it without a law annulling it; he allows that a just law may annul such promises in advance and punish the promisor. Vattel grounds the validity of these promises on the subject's return to his natural rights when he can neither receive the sovereign's orders nor enjoy his protection. He concludes that the sovereign cannot release a subject from a promised ransom and must make him pay it. Grotius leaves the state a power to annul such promises by law, which Vattel's sovereign does not have.
items.passage: Ainsi, quand ce particulier a promis une somme pour sa rançon, loin que le souverain puisse le dégager de sa promesse, il doit l'obliger à la tenir.
items.sourcePassage: Les Loix pourroient sans doute ôter ce pouvoir aux Sujets, tant perpétuels, qu'à ceux qui ne le sont que pour un tems.

items.question: Can a safe-conduct holder transfer the privilege to another person?
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 938 holds that a safe-conduct for goods leaves the owner free to use whatever carriers he wishes. Vattel holds that others may carry the goods only if nothing in their persons makes them justly suspect to the grantor or bars them from his lands. Vattel adds a limiting condition on the choice of carriers.
items.passage: pourvu qu'il n'y ait rien dans leur personne qui puisse les rendre justement suspects à celui qui donne le sauf-conduit
items.sourcePassage: liberum fuit relictum ei, cujus merces sunt, ut in iis transferendis utatur eorum opera, quos voluerit

items.locus: Droit de la guerre et de la paix, Liv. III ch. XXI § 14
items.question: How is the extent of the right given by a safe-conduct to be judged (return, stay)?
items.comment: Grotius, DGP III.21.14, holds that a safe-conduct, as a privilege that harms no third party and costs the grantor little, is to be read broadly rather than narrowly, rejecting restrictions the words would allow unless absurdity or clear indications require them. Vattel measures its extent by the grantor's will alone, as shown by the purpose for which it was given. Vattel drops Grotius's presumption in favour of the broader reading.
items.passage: Le droit que donne un sauf-conduit venant entiérement de la volonté de celui qui l'accorde , cette volonté est la regle sur laquelle on doit en mesurer l'étendue : & la volonté se découvre par la fin pour laquelle le sauf-conduit a été donné.
items.sourcePassage: Ainsi en demeurant dans la propriété des termes, il faut en étendre le sens, plûtôt que le resserrer

items.question: Does a safe-conduct expire on the death or deposition of the grantor?
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 946 holds that a safe-conduct survives the grantor's death because the holder has acquired a true right from a lawful grant which cannot be taken from him. Vattel holds that it survives death or deposition because it is issued by sovereign authority, which does not die. The ground shifts from the holder's acquired right to the continuity of public authority, which leaves room for Vattel's doctrine of revocation in the next section.
items.passage: car il est donné en vertu de l'autorité souveraine , laquelle ne meurt point
items.sourcePassage: Ex hac igitur concessione verum jus acquisivit is, cui commeatus datus (§. 937.), quod ipsi auferri nequit

items.question: May a safe-conduct be revoked, and on what terms?
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 945 holds that even a precarious safe-conduct cannot be revoked so as to remove the holder's security before he reaches a safe place. Vattel requires time to withdraw safely on revocation but allows the holder to be detained for a time, without ill-treatment, to keep him from carrying intelligence to the enemy. Vattel permits a temporary detention that Wolff's rule on security until arrival excludes.
items.passage: Si on le retient quelque tems, comme on feroit tout autre voyageur , pour empêcher qu'il ne porte des lumieres à l'ennemi , ce doit être sans aucun mauvais traitement, et seulement jusqu'à ce que cette raison n'ait plus lieu.
items.sourcePassage: revocatione ea tollinequit, antequam in loco tuto fuerit is, cui concessus

items.question: May a safe-conduct be revoked, and on what terms?
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 946 holds that the holder of a safe-conduct not granted at pleasure acquires a true right which cannot be taken from him. Vattel holds that the grantor or his successor may revoke any safe-conduct for good reasons, since every privilege is revocable when it becomes harmful to the state. Wolff treats the non-precarious safe-conduct as irrevocable and Vattel subjects it to reason of state.
items.passage: Tout privilege peut être révoqué quand il devient nuisible à l'état
items.sourcePassage: Ex hac igitur concessione verum jus acquisivit is, cui commeatus datus (§. 937.), quod ipsi auferri nequit

items.locus: Droit de la guerre et de la paix, Liv. III ch. XXI § 25
items.question: May the right to demand a ransom from a prisoner be transferred to a third party?
items.comment: Grotius, DGP III.21.25, holds that a captor may transfer to another his right to demand a ransom from his prisoner, since natural law permits the alienation of incorporeal rights, and he sets no limit to the transfer. Vattel admits the transfer but holds that the captor, who owes his prisoner fair and humane treatment, should not cede the right without limit to someone who might abuse it until the ransom has been agreed. Once the price is fixed the captor may cede the right to anyone.
items.passage: Mais comme celui qui fait un prisonnier est obligé de le traiter équitablement & avec humanité ( §. 150 ), s'il veut se mettre à couvert de tout reproche, il ne doit point transférer son droit, d'une maniere illimitée, à quelqu'un qui pourroit en abuser : lorsqu'il est convenu avec son prisonnier du prix de la rançon , il peut céder à qui il lui plaira le droit de l'exiger.
items.sourcePassage: je ne doute pourtant pas, que ceux qui ont pris quelcun à la Guerre ne puissent transferer à autrui le droit qu'ils ont d'exiger du Prisonnier une rançon

items.question: May an agreed ransom be rescinded because the prisoner is richer than thought
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 949 holds that an agreed ransom cannot be rescinded because the captive proves richer than believed, and treats fraud as a separate case giving liability for damages. Vattel holds the same rule but grounds the price on the prisoner's rank rather than his wealth, and makes a disguise of rank a fraud that annuls the convention. The difference lies in the remedy for fraud and in the distinction between concealing and disguising rank.
items.passage: Si le prisonnier a, non pas seulement celé , mais déguisé son rang, c'est une fraude qui donne le droit d'annuller la convention.
items.sourcePassage: Alia est ratio, si dolus intercessit, de quo separatim tenetur ad id, quod interest.

items.question: Prisoner released on condition of freeing another, who dies
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 954 holds that a prisoner released on condition of procuring another's release must return to captivity if the other dies before release. Vattel grants this as the strict rule but holds that equity asks the captor to leave him his liberty on payment of a just equivalent. Vattel adds an equitable substitute performance that Wolff does not admit.
items.passage: l'équité semble demander qu'on laisse à ce prisonnier une liberté, laquelle on a bien voulu lui accorder, pourvu qu'il en paie un juste équivalent
items.sourcePassage: is in carcerem redire tenetur, si alter ante dimissionem moriatur, non tenetur, si post dimissionem

items.locus: Droit de la guerre et de la paix, Liv. III ch. XXI § 30
items.question: Must a prisoner released on condition of procuring another's release return to prison if that other dies?
items.comment: Grotius, DGP III.21.30, holds that a prisoner released on condition of procuring another prisoner's release is not bound to return to prison when that other dies first, since no return was stipulated and liberty is too favoured to presume a tacit agreement; he owes only the value of what he promised. Vattel holds that in strict right the prisoner must return to prison, and that only equity suggests leaving him free on payment of a just equivalent. Vattel's strict rule is the result of the Roman jurists set out in Barbeyrac's note, which Grotius rejects as less agreeable to natural law.
items.passage: Il suit, à rigueur, des mêmes principes, qu'un prisonnier relâché à condition d'en faire délivrer un autre, doit retourner en prison, au cas que celui - ci vienne à mourir avant qu'il ait pu lui procurer la liberté.
items.sourcePassage: le Prisonnier, qui a été relâché, n'est point tenu véritablement de se remettre en prison: car cela n'a point été stipulé dans l'accord; & la Liberté est une cause trop favorable pour que l'on présume là-dessus une convention tacite.

items.question: Must the sovereign keep promises made to rebels?
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 1015 holds that whatever the supreme power promises rebels to quell a rebellion must be kept, as promises to an enemy in war are kept. Vattel holds the same rule but allows the sovereign to revoke extorted concessions contrary to the safety of the state, with the consent of the nation given in constitutional form. The exception rests on the salus of the nation as the limit of the sovereign's power to grant.
items.passage: comme il n'est pas en droit de rien faire , de rien accorder , contre cette grande regle de sa conduite et de son pouvoir, il révoquera justement des concessions pernicieuses
items.sourcePassage: Quae rebellibus et tumultuantibus rebellionis aut tumultus sedandi causa promittuntur a summa potestate; ea sunt servanda.

items.locus: Droit de la guerre et de la paix, Liv. III ch. XIX § 7
items.question: Must the prince keep the promises he has made to rebels?
items.comment: Grotius, DGP III.19.7 holds that the sovereign must ordinarily keep agreements made with rebel subjects because the public interest requires it, but may override them by his eminent right when circumstances demand, provided he compensates the subjects affected. Vattel rests the duty on the same inviolability of promises that binds individuals, sovereigns and enemies, and lets the prince revoke only extorted concessions contrary to the welfare of the nation, which he never had power to grant. Vattel makes such revocation depend on the nation's assent given in the forms of the constitution, where Grotius makes it depend on compensation.
items.passage: il révoquera justement des concessions pernicieuses , en s'autorisant del'aveu de la nation, dont il prendra l'avis, de la maniere & dans les formes qui lui seront marquées par la constitution de l'état.
items.sourcePassage: lors même que les circonstances demandent l'usage de ce droit éminent, il faut néanmoins dédommager de quelque autre maniére les Sujets, envers qui on en use

items.question: What is civil war, as against rebellion?
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 1011 defines civil war as war in which subjects take just arms against the ruler, so that civil war and rebellion exclude each other. Vattel rejects this definition and applies the term to any war between members of one political society, including war between factions or rival claimants. For war between subjects and sovereign it suffices that the malcontents have some reason to take arms.
items.passage: L'usage affecte le terme de guerre civile à toute guerre qui se fait entre les membres d'une même société politique
items.sourcePassage: Bellum vero civile dicitur, quo justa arma adversus Rectorem civitatis sumunt subditi.

items.question: What is civil war, as against rebellion?
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 1010 calls rebels those subjects who take unjust arms against the ruler. Vattel restricts rebellion to a rising against legitimate authority destitute of all appearance of justice. A rising with an unjust but colourable cause is rebellion for Wolff and civil war for Vattel.
items.passage: Cette derniere qualification n'est donnée qu'à un soulevement contre l'autorité légitime, destitué de toute apparence de justice.
items.sourcePassage: Rebelles dicuntur subditi, qui arma injusta sumunt adversus Rectorem civitatis.

items.locus: Droit de la guerre et de la paix, Liv. II ch. XVIII § 2
items.question: Does civil war make the two parties independent, so that they are treated as two separate nations?
items.comment: Grotius, DGP II.18.2 regards one nation as two bodies of people for a time only in exceptional civil wars, where the parties are nearly equal and it is uncertain on which side sovereign power lies, or where two claimants to the crown have arguments hard to decide between. Vattel holds that civil war as such produces two independent parties, to be considered as two separate peoples. He applies this even where one side has wrongly resisted legitimate authority, since the parties are divided in fact and have no common judge.
items.passage: Que l'un des deux ait eu tort de rompre l'unité de l'état , de résister à l'autorité légitime, ils n'en sont pas moins divisés de fait.
items.sourcePassage: que le Peuple est divisé en deux Partis presqu'égaux, en sorte qu'on ne sait de quel côté est le Pouvoir Souverain

items.question: How should foreign nations behave in another state's civil war?
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 1011 holds that foreign nations have no judgement over what passes between subjects and their ruler, since they must not meddle in another's government. Vattel accepts the rule of non-interference but holds that, once good offices have failed, nations bound by no treaty may judge the merits for their own conduct and assist the party that appears to have right on its side. Vattel thus admits assistance in civil war on the model of joining a just side in a public war.
items.passage: peuvent sans doute porter leur jugement, pour leur propre conduite, sur le mérite de la cause, et assister le parti qui leur paroîtra avoir le bon droit de son côté
items.sourcePassage: Cum exterarum Gentium non sit judicium de iis, quae inter subditos et Rectorem civitatis alicujus intercedunt, utpote quae sese regimini aliorum inmiscere non debent ( §. 257. )

items.question: Who has power to conclude peace
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 977 holds that only the holders of supreme power can make peace, because the right to make peace belongs to the right of war as one of the rights of majesty. Vattel keeps the link between the two powers but holds that the power of peace does not include the power to grant any conditions, that fundamental laws may limit it, and that a nation may entrust the power of peace to a person or assembly that lacks the power of declaring war. The two powers are separable in Vattel and inseparable in Wolff.
items.passage: La nation qui dispose librement de ses affaires domestiques, de la forme de son gouvernement, peut confier à une personne ou à une assemblée, le pouvoir de faire la paix , quoiqu'elle ne lui ait pas abandonné celui de déclarer la guerre.
items.sourcePassage: Ad jus belli omnino pertinet sicuti jus belli inchoandi et actus bellicos determinandi sive per se, sive per alios; ita etiam jus belli finiendi, consequenter etiam jus pacem pangendi.

items.locus: Droit de la guerre et de la paix, Liv. III ch. XX § 5
items.question: May the prince alienate parts of the state in a peace treaty without the nation's express consent?
items.comment: Grotius, DGP III.20.5 holds that a king who holds his kingdom as usufructuary cannot alienate any part of it by treaty without the consent of the whole people and of the province or town concerned, the latter's consent alone sufficing under extreme necessity. Vattel holds that where the Estates have fallen into disuse the king alone judges what to cede for peace, and that the nation's consent is not required for parts already in the enemy's power. An absolute sovereign may abandon such parts on his own judgement, or at least promise that the nation will never take up arms to recover them.
items.passage: c'est au souverain seul, s'il a l'administration pleine & absolue du gouvernement, le pouvoir de la guerre & de la paix ; c'est, dis-je , à lui seul de juger s'il convient d'abandonner ces parties de l'état, ou de continuer la guerre pour les recouvrer.
items.sourcePassage: Mais, quand il s'agit de l'aliénation de quelque Partie du Roiaume, il faut un double consentement, savoir, celui de tout le Corps du Peuple, & celui de la Province ou de la Ville, que l'on veut aliéner, laquelle ne peut être détachée malgré soi du Corps avec lequel elle étoit unie.

items.locus: Droit de la guerre et de la paix, Liv. II ch. VI § 8
items.question: May the prince alienate parts of the state in a peace treaty without the nation's express consent?
items.comment: Grotius, DGP II.6.8 admits the exceptions of utility and necessity to the ban on alienating parts of the state only as grounds for presuming the consent of the people and of the part from silence over a period, and holds the alienation void where the body or the part manifestly opposes it. Vattel holds that in pressing necessity the prince's alienations are ratified by the nation's silence alone where the nation has kept no ordinary means of express consent and has left the prince absolute power. Vattel treats that silence as a true consent required by the security of treaties, and rejects the plea that the people tolerated the loss of their Estates only through fear.
items.passage: les aliénations que fait le prince pour sauver le reste de l'état, sont censées approuvées & ratifiées par le seul silence de la nation, lorsqu'elle n'a point conservé, dans la forme du gouvernement, quelque moyen aisé & ordinaire de donner son consentement exprès, & qu'elle a abandonné au prince une puissance absolue.
items.sourcePassage: si l'aliénation d'une Partie de l'Etat lui est avantageuse, aussi bien qu'au Corps, le silence pendant un tems, quoi que pas fort long, fait aisément présumer le consentement & du Peuple, & de la Partie aliénée

items.question: Can a king who is a prisoner of war make peace?
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 983 holds that the captive king of a non-patrimonial kingdom may make peace through those to whom he has committed the administration, and failing such a disposition through the heir presumptive. Vattel holds that those called to the regency by the laws of the state take the government and conclude the peace, and that the treaty binds the nation only when ratified by the nation, by the holders of public authority, or by the king after his release. Vattel derives the authority to make peace from the laws of the state, Wolff from the king's delegation or the order of succession.
items.passage: Il faut alors que celui, ou ceux, qui sont appellés à la régence, par les loix de l'état, prennent les rênes du gouvernement.
items.sourcePassage: vel per eos, quibus administrationem imperii commisit: quodsi vero de ea nihil disposuit, pacem facere potest, qui proximam succedendi spem habet

items.question: Can a king who is a prisoner of war make peace?
items.comment: Wolff, Institutiones § 1220 holds that the captive king of a patrimonial kingdom can make peace, because he may dispose of a patrimonial kingdom at will. Vattel rejects the distinction between patrimonial and usufructuary kingdoms and holds that peace is the affair of the nation, so that a captive king can bind the nation only by a treaty ratified by the nation, by the holders of public authority, or by himself after release. Wolff's patrimonial captive king concludes a valid peace alone, Vattel's cannot.
items.passage: mais le traité ne devient obligatoire pour la nation, que quand il est ratifié par elle-même, ou par ceux qui sont dépositaires de l'autorité publique, pendant la captivité du prince, ou enfin par lui-même, après sa délivrance
items.sourcePassage: si regnum fuerit patrimoniale , Rex captivus pacem facere potest

items.question: Can a king who is a prisoner of war make peace?
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 982 holds that the captive king of a patrimonial kingdom can make peace, because he possesses the imperium by right of property and may dispose of it and of each of its rights as he sees fit. Vattel, citing this section, calls the patrimonial kingdom a false and dangerous idea, reduces it to a power to designate a successor or dismember the state for the nation's good, and holds that peace is the affair of the nation, not of the king. Vattel denies the proprietary ground on which Wolff's conclusion rests.
items.passage: Nous croyons avoir détruit cette idée fausse et dangereuse, de royaume patrimonial
items.sourcePassage: Si regnum fuerit patrimoniale, Rex captivus pacem facere potest.

items.locus: Droit de la guerre et de la paix, Liv. III ch. XX § 3
items.question: Can a king who is a prisoner of war validly make peace?
items.comment: Grotius, DGP III.20.3 holds that a captive king cannot make peace only in kingdoms originally established by the people's consent, since the people cannot be presumed to have conferred a power to be exercised while the king is not master of his person, so that a patrimonial king may make peace from captivity. Vattel rejects the distinction between patrimonial and usufructuary kingdoms as false and dangerous, and holds that peace is the affair of the nation under every legitimate government. For Vattel the captive sovereign may negotiate, but the treaty binds the nation only when ratified by the nation, by the regency, or by the king after his release.
items.passage: Nous croyons avoir détruit cette idée fausse & dangereuse, de royaume patrimonial
items.sourcePassage: Il faut dire la même chose d'un Roi (1) Prisonnier, mais seulement (2) dans les Roiaumes originairement établis par le consentement du Peuple

items.question: Must allies be included in the treaty of peace?
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 1009 holds that allies are comprised in the treaty of peace of themselves, because they act in the principal's name and the amnesty implicit in every peace extends to them. Vattel holds that the principal party is bound in justice to include its allies, and that the treaty binds the allies only so far as they accept it, unless they gave full powers to treat for them. Inclusion is automatic in Wolff and a duty of the principal subject to the allies' consent in Vattel.
items.passage: Mais le traité de la partie principale n'oblige ses alliés qu'autant qu'ils veulent bien l'accepter, à moins qu'ils ne luiayent donné tout pouvoir de traiter pour eux.
items.sourcePassage: In foedere igitur pacis iidem etiam comprehenduntur.

items.locus: Droit de la guerre et de la paix, Liv. III ch. XX § 16
items.question: Which claims fall outside the peace transaction or amnesty (prior debts and injuries unrelated to the war, movables)?
items.comment: Grotius, DGP III.20.16 holds that debts between private persons contracted before the war are not extinguished by the peace, since war only suspends their exaction, and confines the presumption that pre-war rights survive to rights arising from contract. Vattel holds that claims founded on a debt or on an injury prior to the war survive the treaty unless it expressly extinguishes all pretensions, provided they had no part in the causes of the war. Vattel makes the claim's relation to the war the test, not its source in contract, so that claims for unrelated pre-war injuries survive, where Grotius, DGP III.20.17-18 presumes the right to punish pre-war injuries remitted by the peace.
items.passage: Ainsi des répétitions fondées sur une dette, ou sur une injure antérieure à la guerre , qui n'a eu aucune part aux raisons qui l'ont fait entreprendre , demeurent en leur entier , & ne sont point abolies prr le traité
items.sourcePassage: cela doit pourtant s'entendre des droits qui naissent d'un Contract, où il y auroit autrement de la lézion.

items.question: Whether impossibility excuses non-performance of a treaty promise
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 665 holds that an ally engaged in its own war is not obliged to furnish what it needs itself, and that the promisor's own judgment decides whether it can furnish it. Vattel admits only an excuse founded on a real and insurmountable impediment and holds that a promise which can be fulfilled later is suspended, so that arrears are owed once the impediment ceases. Wolff's excuse releases the obligation, Vattel's defers it where performance remains possible.
items.passage: Si la promesse peut être remplie en une autre occasion , il faut accorder un délai convenable.
items.sourcePassage: si foederatus ipse bello implicitus iis indiget, quae vi foederis praestanda forent foederato, ad ea praestanda non obligatur

items.question: Can duress or fear be pleaded to escape a peace treaty?
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 1035 holds that force or fear never invalidates a treaty of peace, because the amnesty tacitly waives the exception and the parties disregard whether the fear was just or unjust. Vattel accepts the rule for ordinary treaties but holds that a forced submission to conditions contrary to justice and humanity imposed by an unjust conqueror is not a peace and may be thrown off at the first opportunity. Vattel makes the injustice of the constraint decisive where Wolff declares it irrelevant.
items.passage: Si jamais l'exception de la contrainte peut être alléguée, c'est contre un acte, qui ne mérite pas le nom de traité de paix, contre une soumission forcée à des conditions , qui blessent également la justice et tous les devoirs de l'humanité.
items.sourcePassage: a transigentibus nec attenditur, utrum justo, an injusto metu ad pacem sub hisce conditionibus faciendam pars alterutra permoveatur

items.locus: Droit de la guerre et de la paix, Liv. III ch. XIX § 11
items.question: Can a nation free itself from a peace treaty by pleading that it was extorted by fear or force?
items.comment: Grotius, DGP III.19.11 holds that promises made in a solemn war or to end it cannot be annulled on the plea of unjust fear, because the law of nations deems that fear just on both sides so that wars may be ended, and leaves the unjust victor bound only in conscience not to keep what he extorted. Vattel denies the plea of fear on the ground of the security of peace treaties and of the nation's free choice of a limited loss, but excepts a forced submission imposed by a conqueror who attacked without any pretext, which is oppression and not peace and may be thrown off at the first occasion. Vattel follows Barbeyrac's note against Grotius in distinguishing a war waged without any cause from one waged on a plausible pretext.
items.passage: Si jamais l'exception de la contrainte peut être alléguée, c'est contre un acte, qui ne mérite pas le nom de traité de paix, contre une soumission forcée à des conditions , qui blessent également la justice & tous les devoirs de l'humanité.
items.sourcePassage: qu'elles (1) ne peuvent point être annullées sous prétexte d'une crainte injuste, sans le consentement de celui-là même à qui l'on a promis

items.locus: Droit de la guerre et de la paix, Liv. III ch. XIX § 12
items.question: Can a nation free itself from a peace treaty by pleading that it was extorted by fear or force?
items.comment: Grotius, DGP III.19.12 limits the rule that fear counts as just on both sides in a solemn war to fear tolerated by the law of nations, and leaves promises extorted by threats such as rape or breach of faith to natural law alone. Vattel rejects the plea of fear against a peace treaty on the ground of the common safety of treaties and the free choice of the vanquished, and admits it only against a forced submission to unjust and inhuman conditions imposed by an unjust conqueror. Grotius's exception turns on the unlawful means of coercion, Vattel's on the injustice of the war and of the terms.
items.passage: Si jamais l'exception de la contrainte peut être alléguée, c'est contre un acte, qui ne mérite pas le nom de traité de paix, contre une soumission forcée à des conditions , qui blessent également la justice & tous les devoirs de l'humanité.
items.sourcePassage: cela ne doit s'entendre que (1) d'une crainte tolérée par le Droit des Gens

items.question: Does taking arms for a new cause break the peace treaty?
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 1025 holds that war for a new cause does not break the peace, since the treaty only bars renewed war over the cause already settled. Vattel holds that neither the party taking up arms nor the party refusing satisfaction is reputed to break the treaty, whether the new ground is just or not, provided both the complaint and the refusal have some colour of right. The colour-of-right proviso makes the rule depend on the question being litigious, a condition absent from Wolff.
items.passage: ni celui qui en prend occasion de courrir aux armes, ni celui qui refuse satisfaction, n'est réputé rompre le traité de paix, pourvû que le sujet de plainte, et le refus de satisfaction aient de part et d'autre au moins quelque couleur
items.sourcePassage: Quodsi ergo bellum inferatur ob novam causam, id contra pactionem pacis non fit, consequenter nec pax rumpitur

items.question: Does later allying with the enemy of one's peace partner break the peace treaty?
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 1026 holds that a later war alliance against one's former enemy does not break the peace and cannot be charged as perfidy unless the treaty expressly forbids it. Vattel accepts the rule only on the supposition that the new allies have a plausible cause and one has just reasons to support them. Joining them at the outbreak of their war without such reasons is for Vattel a pretext to evade the treaty and a perfidious breach of it.
items.passage: car s'il en étoit autrement, s'allier avec eux, justement lorsqu'ils vont entrer en guerre, ou lorsqu'ils l'ont commencée, ce seroit manifestement chercher un prétexte pour éluder le traité de paix, ce seroit le rompre avec une artificieuse perfidie
items.sourcePassage: nec hunc te perfidiae accusare posse, nisi pax ita inita fuerit, ne posthac ulli adversus alterum in bello te associes

items.locus: Droit de la guerre et de la paix, Liv. III ch. XX § 32
items.question: Does lawful self-defence break a peace treaty, and how far may offenders be pursued onto foreign soil?
items.comment: Grotius, DGP III.20.32 allows offenders to be pursued without judicial process only when they are habitual wrongdoers such as pirates, presumed to act against their sovereign's will and beyond the reach of justice, and permits their punishment as if their sovereign had delivered them up. Vattel allows armed pursuit into the neighbouring country whenever the culprits may escape, as with unknown raiders, and only until they are seized. Vattel grounds the pursuit on legitimate defence instead of a presumed surrender by the sovereign, and drops the right to punish.
items.passage: Si l'on a lieu de craindre que les coupables n'échappent ; si, par exemple, des inconnus, d'un pays voisin, ont fait irruption sur nos terres, nous sommes en droit de les poursuivre chez eux à main armée, jusquesà-ce qu'ils soient saisis
items.sourcePassage: on peut, sans autre forme de procès, courir après eux, pour leur enlever son bien, & pour les punir même, comme s'ils avoient été livrez entre nos mains par leur Souverain

items.locus: Droit de la guerre et de la paix, Liv. III ch. XX § 40
items.question: Which acts contrary to the particular nature (friendship) of a peace treaty break it?
items.comment: Grotius, DGP III.20.40 holds that acts against friendship break a peace made on that condition, but presumes that an injury to the partner's kin or subjects is not aimed at the partner unless a manifest design to insult him appears. Vattel lists harsh treatment of the other nation's subjects among acts evidently contrary to friendship, with no such presumption. The difference lies in Grotius's rule of benign construction, which Vattel drops.
items.passage: Favoriser les ennemis d'une nation, traiter durement ses sujets, la gêner sans raison dans son commerce
items.sourcePassage: l'injure ne sera point censée faite à lui-même, à moins qu'on n'aît eu un dessein manifeste de l'insulter ou de l'outrager par là indirectement

items.question: Does violation of a single article break the whole treaty?
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 1023 holds that a peace broken in diverse, unconnected articles endures in the remaining articles, since each diverse article forms a separate peace. Vattel rejects the distinction between connected and diverse articles and follows Grotius in treating all articles of one treaty as reciprocal conditions. For Vattel the violation of a single article affects the whole treaty unless an express clause provides otherwise.
items.passage: Mais si cette clause ne se trouve pas expressément dans le traité de paix, un seul article violé donne atteinte au traité entier
items.sourcePassage: si pax rumpitur in articulis diversis, in caeteris durat

items.question: Does violation of a single article break the whole treaty?
items.comment: Wolff, Institutiones § 1230 holds that a peace broken in diverse articles subsists in the others, and that only breach of connected articles releases the other party. Vattel rejects the distinction between connected and diverse articles and treats all articles as mutual conditions. For Vattel a single violated article affects the whole treaty unless the treaty expressly provides otherwise.
items.passage: Mais si cette clause ne se trouve pas expressément dans le traité de paix, un seul article violé donne atteinte au traité entier
items.sourcePassage: si pax rumpitur in articulis diversis, eam in ceteris durare

items.question: Should articles be distinguished by importance when one is violated?
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 1024 holds that the peace is broken by violation of minor heads, on the ground that a promise binds because it is promised, not because of the weight of its object. Vattel holds that in strict right the violation of the least article releases the injured party from all the others, on the ground that all articles are linked as conditions. Vattel adds that the duties of charity and love of peace make it improper always to break a treaty for the slightest grievance.
items.passage: A rigueur de droit, la violation du moindre article dispense la partie lésée de l'observation des autres , puisque tous, comme nous venons de le voir, sont liés les uns aux autres, en forme de conditions.
items.sourcePassage: Nimirum fides ut sancta sit, consequenter quod promissum est inviolabile ( §. 546. ), non inde venit, quod res majoris momenti promissa, sed quia promissa.

items.locus: Droit de la guerre et de la paix, Liv. III ch. XX § 37
items.question: What follows when performance of an article becomes impossible through insurmountable obstacle?
items.comment: Grotius, DGP III.20.37 holds that impossibility of performance does not break the peace, and leaves the other party the choice of waiting, demanding the value, or releasing itself from the corresponding engagements. Vattel denies the other party the right to break the treaty and requires it to accept compensation where compensation is due and practicable, but declares the whole treaty void when it was evidently made for the impossible thing alone. Grotius's option of release from the equivalent engagements disappears, and Vattel adds a ground of total nullity that Grotius does not state.
items.passage: l'autre partie ne peut prendre occasion de son impuissance, pour rompre le traité; mais elle doit accepter un dédommagement, s'il y a lieu à dédommagement, & s'il est praticable
items.sourcePassage: il doit être au choix de l'autre Partie, ou d'attendre quelque tems l'effet de ce qu'on lui avoit promis; s'il y a encore quelque espérance que la chose devienne possible, ou d'exiger la valeur de ce qui avoit été stipulé, ou bien de se liberer des engagemens réciproques ou équivalens à l'Article de la Paix

items.question: Do violations of a peace treaty by allies break the peace for the other party?
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 1027 holds that acts of former allies contrary to the peace do not break it for you, since they cease to be allies at the peace and their acts cannot be imputed to you. Vattel holds that the treaty subsists for the faithful ally only provided he does not support the cause of the perfidious allies. Aid not owed to them makes him a party to their breach, while intervention to secure reparation and prevent their ruin remains lawful.
items.passage: Le traité subsiste pour lui dans toute sa force , pourvu qu'il n'entreprenne point de soutenir la cause de ces alliés perfides.
items.sourcePassage: Si qui fuerant in bello socii, aut subditi tui sine consensu tuo, vel subsecuta ratihabitione faciant, quod est contra pactionem pacis; pax non rumpitur.

items.question: Must a sovereign receive the minister of a friendly power?
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 1045 holds that ambassadors must be admitted, since the sender has a perfect right of legation and refusal is an injury unless a duty of the nation to itself collides. Vattel holds that a sovereign may not refuse to hear the minister of a friendly power without very particular reasons, but may keep him at a place on the frontier. For Vattel the sender's claim is satisfied by a hearing, not by admission into the country.
items.passage: il suffit qu'on l'entende ; c'est tout ce qu'il peut prétendre.
items.sourcePassage: si non admittuntur, mittenti injuria fit, nisi id fiat in casu collisionis officiorum Gentis erga seipsam et erga Gentes alias

items.question: Must a sovereign tolerate permanent resident ministers?
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 1048 holds that resident embassies belong only to customary law, so any nation may withdraw its tacit consent and stand on its own judgment. Vattel agrees that there is no obligation to suffer permanent ministers but holds that the custom is now so established that very good reasons must be alleged to refuse them without offence. Vattel turns Wolff's free withdrawal into a refusal that needs a justifying reason.
items.passage: La coutume d'entretenir par-tout des ministres continuellement résidens , est aujourd'hui si bien établie , qu'il faut alléguer de très-bonnes raisons pour refuser de s'y prêter sans offenser personne.
items.sourcePassage: consequenter si qua eo diutius stare nolit, ipsi ut suo stet judicio permittendum

items.question: Must a sovereign tolerate permanent resident ministers?
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 1049 holds that resident ministers may be refused without injury and that no particular right or reason is needed to refuse them. Vattel holds that refusal is lawful but that the established custom requires very good reasons, drawn from particular conjunctures or from the constitution of the state, to refuse without offence. The point of difference is whether a refusal must be justified.
items.passage: La coutume d'entretenir par-tout des ministres continuellement résidens , est aujourd'hui si bien établie , qu'il faut alléguer de très-bonnes raisons pour refuser de s'y prêter sans offenser personne.
items.sourcePassage: Quare nec peculiari quodam jure opus est, quo eos non admittere liceat.

items.locus: Droit de la guerre et de la paix, Liv. II ch. XVIII § 3
items.question: Must a state accept permanent resident ministers?
items.comment: Grotius, DGP II.18.3 holds that ordinary embassies with permanent residence may freely be refused, since antiquity did without them. Vattel agrees that there is no obligation to admit resident ministers, but holds that the custom is now so established that a state needs very good reasons to refuse them without giving offence. Vattel turns established custom into a condition on refusal that Grotius does not impose.
items.passage: La coutume d'entretenir par-tout des ministres continuellement résidens , est aujourd'hui si bien établie , qu'il faut alléguer de très-bonnes raisons pour refuser de s'y prêter sans offenser personne.
items.sourcePassage: Pour ce qui est des Ambassades ordinaires & accompagnées d'une résidence perpétuelle , dont l'usage est aujourdhui fort fréquent, on peut fort bien les refuser.

items.question: Whether consuls, agents, deputies and commissaries are public ministers, and what they are owed
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 1043 holds that agents, even when entrusted with minor public business, enjoy only the law of foreigners or, if citizens, the law of other citizens. Vattel holds that agents are not public ministers but are owed a more particular protection than other foreigners or citizens, and that an agent sent with letters of credence for public affairs is a public minister whatever his title.
items.passage: Mais on leur doit une protection plus particuliere qu'à d'autres étrangers ou citoyens , et quelques égards en considération du prince qu'ils servent.
items.sourcePassage: Si enim suntperegrini, jure non alio utuntur quam peregrinorum in territorio alieno degentium: si vero sunt cives, quales esse possunt, eodem jure censentur, quo cives alii.

items.question: What instructions are and whether a minister's engagements bind his principal
items.comment: Wolff, Institutiones § 553 holds that what a mandatary does within the limits of a manifest mandate binds the principal, and that the principal must ratify what was done within a secret mandate. Vattel holds that by established usage a minister's engagements have no force between sovereigns unless ratified by his principal. Vattel sets aside the natural-law rule of mandate and makes ratification the condition of binding force.
items.passage: par un usage sagement établi les engagemens dans lesquels un ministre peut entrer , n'ont aujourd'hui aucune force entre les souverains , s'ils ne sont ratifiés par son principal
items.sourcePassage: consequenter promittendo te huic et acceptando hunc tibi obligat

items.question: Whether foreign ministers are independent of the jurisdiction of the state of residence, and on what ground
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 1060 holds that by the natural law of nations envoys, their retinue and effects are subject to the civil and criminal jurisdiction of the place as to private acts. Vattel holds that the public minister must be independent of the sovereign authority and jurisdiction of the country in civil and criminal matters, and that natural law requires this independence.
items.passage: Il faut donc, pour assurer le succès de son ministere, qu'il soit indépendant de l'autorité souveraine de la jurisdiction du pays, tant pour le civil que pour le criminel.
items.sourcePassage: legati quoque quoad actus privatos cum comitatu et vasis seu rebus suis jure Gentium naturali jurisdictioni loci subsunt tam civili, quam criminali

items.question: Whether foreign ministers are independent of the jurisdiction of the state of residence, and on what ground
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 1059 holds that extraterritoriality belongs neither to the natural nor to the voluntary law of nations and can be acquired only by express or tacit pact. Vattel, citing this section, holds that the independence of ministers follows from the natural obligation to admit them with the privileges their function requires, with tacit convention only adding force. Wolff makes pact the sole ground; Vattel makes it a supplement to natural law.
items.passage: et voilà, entre les deux princes, une convention tacite, qui donne une nouvelle force à l'obligation naturelle
items.sourcePassage: consequenter ea aliter acquiri nequit, quam ex pacto sive expresso, sive tacito

items.question: How a minister guilty of common offences against subjects is to be dealt with
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 1065 holds that the sanctity of legates does not exempt them from the jurisdiction of the receiving sovereign in their private acts, so that their delicts may call for public punishment. Vattel holds the ambassador independent of the ordinary magistrates, so that offended subjects must apply to their own sovereign, who seeks justice from the ambassador's master and may order the minister to leave. The difference lies in whether local courts may act against the ambassador at all.
items.passage: les sujets offensés ne doivent point recourir aux magistrats ordinaires , de la jurisdiction desquels l'ambassadeur est indépendant
items.sourcePassage: ejus potius jurisdictioni subsint quoad actiones suas privatas

items.locus: Droit de la guerre et de la paix, Liv. II ch. XVIII § 4
items.question: What may be done to a conspiring ambassador as the danger requires (arrest, killing)?
items.comment: Grotius, DGP II.18.4 allows an ambassador to be arrested and interrogated in pressing danger to the state, and allows him to be killed only when he resorts to armed force, by the natural right of defence. Vattel allows an ambassador who directs a conspiracy to be arrested and even put to death if that is necessary to defeat it. Vattel grounds this on the safety of the state and on a perfect right of defence created by the ambassador's own acts, by which he forfeits the protection of the law of nations.
items.passage: S'il étoit nécessaire , pour déconcerter & prévenir une conjuration, d'arrêter , de faire périr même un ambassadeur qui l'anime & la dirige, je ne vois pas qu'il y eût à balancer
items.sourcePassage: Que si un Ambassadeur entreprend quelque chose à main armée, on peut alors sans contredit le faire mourir, non en forme de punition, mais en usant du droit naturel de la Défense.

items.locus: Droit de la guerre et de la paix, Liv. II ch. XVIII § 7
items.question: May reprisals be taken against an ambassador?
items.comment: Grotius, DGP II.18.7 denies any right of reprisal against an ambassador, since the law of nations protects the ambassador himself by a tacit agreement, and approves the Romans who released Carthaginian envoys after Carthage had ill-treated or put in chains envoys of Rome. Vattel forbids reprisals against an innocent minister as acts unlawful in themselves, but permits arresting the envoy of a prince who has arrested ours, without other ill-treatment, as a pledge for our envoy's life and liberty. Grotius admits no such exception.
items.passage: quand un prince, violant le droit des gens, a fait arrêter notre ambassadeur, nous pouvons arrêter & retenir le sien, afin d'assurer par ce gage, la vie & la liberté du nôtre.
items.sourcePassage: On est censé traiter aussi tacitement avec eux: & ainsi on leur fait du tort en les maltraitant, lors même qu'on n'en fait aucun à leur Maître.

items.locus: Droit de la guerre et de la paix, Liv. II ch. XVIII § 4
